courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Internet, Digital Media and Information Society
courses.description:
(UGEC2624 is double-coded with COMM2940.)

This course aims to examine a number of key issues that are closely related to developments in Internet and digital media. The advent of communication technologies has brought tremendous changes to media environments. Media convergence and participatory culture are two most notable emerging trends that have contributed to new forms of media production and consumption. Students will be introduced to key concepts and perspectives in appreciating, analyzing and evaluating such trends. Through case studies about social media, streaming entertainment, Internet celebrities, networked social movements and digital surveillance culture, etc, students will review the many tacit assumptions about Internet in their everyday life.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2624 is double-coded with COMM2940.Not for Journalism and Communication; Global Communication Majors; and students who have taken COMM2940. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1 Phenomena, problems and issues**

In this introductory class, we will examine a few recent viral cases in social media and discuss two recurring themes, namely convergence and participation, in this course.

* *Week 2 When old media were new…**

In this class, we will dive into a few key episodes in the history of communication technologies. We will review and discuss how various factors have contributed to the invention and development of communication fads.

* *Week 3 Mediated memories: How we remember and are remembered?**

Communication technologies have been important memory devices in human history. We will trace how communication technologies co-evolved with memory practices.

* *Week 4 Social media: How we connect and are connected?**

What media are not “social media”? Media always facilitate networking in different forms. We will reconsider what differentiates the social media we know of today from previous generations of social media.

* *Week 5 Dating apps and romance**

The meanings of ‘romance’ and ‘intimacy’ have undergone sweeping changes with the advent of dating apps in smartphones. In this class, we will examine the features of these apps and uncover their assumptions underlying ‘love’.

* *Week 6 MOOC and learning**

Massive Open Online Courses are introducing new forms of teaching, learning and academic accreditation. In a broader sense, how has Internet transformed learning? We will critically evaluate some popular claims in this aspect.

* *Week 7 KOL and public opinions**

Key Opinion Leaders are also known as social influencers or sometimes internet celebrities. They are seen to exert increasing influence in ‘public opinions’ or ‘public sentiments’.　In this class, we will revisit earlier communication theory regarding two-step flow of information and see how Internet has brought new practices in shaping public opinions.

* *Week 8 Streaming media and entertainment**

In this class, we will focus on the case of streaming media and discuss how entertainment is changed in the Internet era. We will also consider how this in turn affects the production, distribution and consumption of media products.

* *Week 9 - 10 Haters and comment culture**

Comment culture is a notable Internet phenomenon. Instead of looking at ‘likes’, we focus on the mechanisms behind ‘dislikes’ and the behaviors of ‘haters’.

* *Week 11 Protest mobilization and social movements**

Internet is seen to be a key factor in protest mobilization. We will examine some key elements in social movements and discuss how social media, for example, have contributed (or not) in the mobilization process.

* *Week 12 Surveillance and sensor society**

The classic ‘big brother’ thesis is discussed with a careful consideration of many emerging practices in surveillance and self-surveillance. The idea of ‘sensor society’ will be introduced to see how we are (in)voluntarily contributing to a productive surveillance culture.

* *Week 13 Hello future!**

In this final class, we will reconsider the two central themes of convergence and participation and make both informed and wild guesses for the future.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Economic Insecurity and Social Security in Global Contexts
courses.description:
(UGEC2631 is double-coded with SOWK2160.)

This course aims at analyzing economic insecurity from a global perspective and introducing social security as a societal measure to combat economic insecurity. Specifically, this course will examine the sources of economic insecurity of the individual and the relationship between globalization and economic insecurity. It will also discuss the philosophy, development, characteristics and functions of different types of social security measures in different countries and analyze current debates on the future development of social security in national and cross-national perspective.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2631 is double-coded with SOWK2160. 
Not for Social Work Majors; and students who have taken SOWK2160. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Insecurity and economic insecurity**
1. Meaning and types of insecurity in the globalised world
2. Economic insecurity – definition, sources and impact
3. Economic and financial globalization and economic insecurity

* *Understanding global poverty**

1. Concepts and definitions

2. Theories of poverty causation

3. Measuring poverty, poverty incidence and trends

4. Strategies to combat poverty and economic insecurity

5. Global overview of economic insecurity and poverty

6. Global goals, frameworks and strategies in eradicating poverty and economic insecurity

* *Social security: a strategy to combat poverty and economic insecurity**

1. Concept, definitions, objectives and scope

2. Historical trends in social security development

3. Types and branches of social security provisions and their underpinning values and principles

4. Structural components of social security provisions

5. Welfare ideologies and social security systems

6. Global overview of social security practices

7. Development and provisions of social security in Hong Kong in comparison with other countries and jurisdictions – similarities and differences

* *Old age and economic insecurity**

1. A global perspective on economic insecurity and poverty in old age

2. Measures to relieve economic insecurity and hardship in old age – options, strengths and weaknesses

3. Mandatory Provident Fund Vs. Old Age Pension Scheme

4. Balancing fiscal viability and financial security of old age

* *Unemployment, underemployment and economic insecurity**

1. Unemployment & underemployment: global trends & regional characteristics

2. Economic insecurity associated with unemployment and underemployment

3. Measures to combat economic insecurity associated with unemployment and underemployment – social security, active labour market policies & community economic development – local and overseas

4. The working poor

* *Economic insecurity arising from sickness; & Health Care**

1. Economic insecurity associated with sickness and health risks

2. Access to affordable and sustainable health care – problems and options

* *Conclusion**

1. Contributions, criticisms and issues of social security programs in combating economic insecurity and global poverty

2. Debates and controversies on future development of social security in national and cross-national perspective

3. Integration of social security and other public and social measures

courses.title: Media, Sex and Violence
courses.description:
(UGEC2632 is double-coded with COMM2920.)

This course is designed to provide students with some familiarily with and critical perspectives on media representations of violence, social conflict, sex, sexuality and gender roles. Efforts will be made to explore the potential impact of such media representations on conflicts, violence, crimes and sexual practices in the real world.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2632 is double-coded with COMM2920. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM2920. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Expected Learning Outcomes**

1. To familiarize students with concepts which interrogate the interplay between modern media and the production, reproduction and transformation of the contemporary social order.

2. To be able to understand and critique the role of the media in sustaining power and inequalities in contemporary societies.

3. To sensitize students to the potential and obstacles posed by media production and consumption for social change.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Course Objective**

Media representation is the construction of symbols that shape, maintain, reinforce, repair, perpetuate and transform social reality. This course studies the conditions for producing a particular set of media representation and how it perpetuates the current power structure. How the progressive ideas of sex and violence can enter the social realm of discussion through media representation will also be studied.

The course explores media representation as a powerful tool in perpetuating certain social reality in the following aspects: (1) it is additive to existing cultural values; (2) it supplements face-to-fact communication; and (3)the representation is monopolized (one-sided). The course also aims to sharpen students' sensitivity to the social reality that media representation of sex and violence as a commercial product is largely an outcome of the reliance of media organizations on advertising money as the funding source. In other words, the imperative of such media representation (a commercial product) is rooted in the particular socio-economic structures of commercial media organization.

The notion of "power" will also be studied in the following aspects: (1) it shapes our understanding of gender roles and "just" use of violence; (2) media organization is structurally more resourceful than the audience; (3)media representation of sex and violence is carefully constructed to appear as the "normal"/"natural"; and (4) the constructive nature of media representation is hidden.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Media and Social Development in Mainland China
courses.description:
(UGEC2634 is double-coded with COMM2140.)

The course is designed around two major themes, namely media and social development in Mainland China since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. Using key concepts and theories from the political economy of media and developmental communication studies, it introduces students to different periods of media reform and social change from the era of Chairman Mao to the period of "harmonious society". Emphasis is attached to post-1989 media regulatory systems, media industrialization, and their influence on the meeting of such developmental goals as poverty alleviation, democratization, and communication empowerment.

The course will examine Mainland China's key media sectors including the printing press (newspapers and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked communication tools (Internet and mobile phone) as well as alternative social formations through Internet activism, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and transnational developmental projects. The course will identify and discuss several ongoing debates, and the ensuing actions, held by different stakeholders, including governmental officials, media producers, educators, activists, international agencies, and the general audiences. Wider implications to public policy will be identified. There will also be discussions of current affairs related to media and social development in the country.

Students will be able to describe the key characteristics of contemporary Mainland Chinese media and their roles in facilitating or obstructing development towards the ideals of a "new China".
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2634 is double-coded with COMM2140. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM2140. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be able to describe key characteristics of media in Mainland China.

2. Students will be able to discuss how media influences social development and how new social formations trigger media reform in Mainland China.

3. Students will be able to identify phases of media and social development in Mainland China and differentiate policymaking rationales in different media sectors (printing, broadcasting, networked media) and types of social movements.

4. Students will be able to discuss competing arguments about the role of media reform in China's modernization drive.

5. Students will be able to produce a media text that offers a critique to one of the historical periods, media industries, or controversial issues covered in the course.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course consists of five main parts: (I) theories of media, communication and social development (week 1 and 2); (II) history of media transformation in Mainland China since 1949 (week 3 and 4); (III) key media sectors (week 5 to 7); (IV) social movements and campaigns (week 8 to 10); and (V) institutional stakeholders (week 11 and 12). In each part, there will be a mixture of conceptual and practical information, of consensus and controversies, and of historical knowledge and current affairs. The class will also look at different disadvantaged social groups and their relationship with various media sectors and stakeholders both within and outside officialdom.

The following is an outline of the course:

* *Week 1 Introduction: Ideals of "New China"**

The first class will introduce students to (a) the pursuit of a "New China" that gave legitimacy to the rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) since the May Fourth Movement, and (b) classical theories of media and national development between 1950s and 1980s. It will also discuss the concept of 'social development' and give an overview of the course's core content.

* Key concepts: "New China", nation building, communication and development*

* *Week 2 Communist Media Theories: Political Control and Social Development**

This class discusses Leninist press theory, its evolution in the Chinese party-state, and the rationale behind this historical transformation, including politico-economic considerations as well as trends in cultural and technological change. Key ideas of the mass line and ICTD (information and communication technologies and development) will also be discussed in the case of rural development.

* Key concepts: Leninist press theory, party-state, political control, the mass line, ICTD, rural development*

* *Week 3 and 4 Past and Present**

These two classes differentiate media and social development in Mainland China into three historical periods: 1949-1978; 1978-1989; and 1989-date. What defines these periods? How are they different? Did previous periods pave the way for later trends of marketization and partial liberalization in the post-1989 era?

* Key concepts: The Maoist era, pre-1989 media reform, post-1989 reform, marketization, partial liberalization*

* *Weeks 5 to 7 Key Media Sectors**

Zooming into China's printing media (newspaper and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked media (Internet and mobile phone), these three classes provide a sector-specific analysis of China's media systems and their contributions to meeting goals of social development. Issues of censorship and regulation will be introduced. Debates on the digital divide will also be discussed.

* Key concepts: printing media, film, broadcasting media, networked media, censorship, regulation, digital divide*

* *Weeks 8 to 10 Social Movements and Campaigns**

These three classes focus on official efforts to modernize China using traditional and new media channels as well as alternative communication empowerment projects such as those led by domestic labor NGOs, environmental groups, and transnational civil society players. Studies in minority-nationality regions and with regard to disadvantaged groups such as women will be discussed along with the official project of "constructing new socialist countryside".

* Key concepts: "constructing new socialist countryside", activism, empowerment, feminist activism, environmental movement, minority nationalities, transnational civil society*

* *Week 11 and 12 Institutional Stakeholders**

We will first return to China's media regulatory frameworks centered on the CCP's Central Propaganda Division (CPD) as well as several ministry-level governing bodies whose bureaucratic systems extend to lower levels of the party-state. Then in Week 12, we will look into China's journalism education system as another key institutional stakeholder. To what extent are the regulators and educators facilitating or hindering overall social development? Why? How could they do better? How could college students in Hong Kong play a meaningful role interacting with the stakeholders?

* Key concepts: CPD, local state, media governance, journalism education, democratization*

* *Week 13 Student Group Presentations and Course Wrap-Up**

Students will present their final projects in the last class, which will end with the instructor's wrap-up of the course.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Social Media and Crisis Communication
courses.description:
(UGEC2636 is double-coded with COMM2813.)

With the advent of the new media technology, new forms of organizational crisis emerge. They are called Internet-mediated crises. A major difference between the Internet-mediated crises and the traditional crises lies in the intensive interactivity, collectivity, simultaneity and dialogic sphericity of the former. This very nature of Internet-mediated crisis makes it all the more hard to handle. A specialized and critical function of the public relations practice is the management of crisis.

This course covers two major levels. The first level takes on a functionalism approach to crisis management. The second level takes on a more critical approach in public relations. Students will learn how crisis reflects complicity and dynamism between citizens and organizations in modern societies. They will acquire an enhanced appreciation of communication that can be brought to bear in such crisis situations and a greater familiarity with the interactivity of an organization and its stakeholders as well as the environments in times of crises. They will also gain more sensitivity in public demands of socially responsible practices in the business contexts.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2636 is double-coded with COMM2813. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM2813. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.course_syllabus:
The following is an outline of the course:

Week 1 Introduction: What is a crisis?

The course will begin with a question: “what is a crisis?” This is a fundamental question in crisis communication and management because failure in spotting a crisis (i.e., treating a crisis as a regular problem, or vice versa) may bring substantial internal and external threats to the organizations. Several crisis and non-crisis cases will be used for comparisons and discussions. At the end of the class, the students should be able to grasp the core characteristics of a crisis and the types of crisis commonly occurred in modern societies.

Key concepts: Crisis vs. problem, types of crisis, crisis impacts

Week 2 The stakeholder theory and the four models of public relations

The class teaches Freeman (1984)’s stakeholder theory. It proffers the students an overview of the scope of the stakeholder groups that an organization may need to handle in crisis communication and communication. It then introduces Grunig and Hunt’s (1984) four models of public relations to give students a framework in viewing the relationships between organizations and stakeholders. Consequences of ignoring these relationships will be examined through the use of real crisis cases.

Key concepts: The stakeholder theory, four models of public relations

Week 3 The public, the media and the new media

The class examines the evolution of the public demand and expectation on organizations in general and in times of crisis. The role of the media in shaping public opinion in crisis is also discussed. It also examines the impact of the advent of the new media technology on crisis communication and management. Online public forums on crisis cases will be studied.

Key concepts: The critical mass, the media, the new media, the social media

Week 4 Blog-related crisis in modern societies.

Blog-related crises include crises initiated or facilitated by personal blogs. The class examines rumor and fact types of blog-related crises. To demonstrate, several recent examples are used illustrate the huge impact of public comments on blogs. Factors that contribute to effective blog-related crisis management are discussed.

Key concepts: blogs, word-of-mouth and blogosphere

Week 5 and 6 Pre-crisis planning

The class teaches a crucial stage in crisis management: Pre-crisis alert and planning.

A good pre-crisis preparation may save an organization from a crisis. As such, students will be taught risk assessment, early detection and planning in the pre-crisis stage. Organizational structures and cultures that facilitate down-up reporting are necessary in early detection. Organizations that are particularly prone to crisis will be discussed. The importance of pre-crisis detection on the Internet and tools for monitoring will also be discussed.

Key concepts: pre-crisis stage, crisis planning, risk assessment, organizational structures, organizational cultures

Week 7 and 8 Crisis communication and management

Benoit’s (1995) image restoration theory and Coombs’ (1999) on-going crisis theory will be used to build theoretical frameworks in conceptualizing crisis communication and management. The class also examines the principles in making news to give students some guidelines about what to say and do in times of crisis, especially upon media enquiry. Good and bad examples of crisis communication management will be used for comparison and contrast.

Key concepts: crisis communication and management, image restoration theory, ongoing crisis, the making of news

Week 9 and 10 Post-crisis communication

Post-crisis communication is as important as crisis management because it determines how successful an organization is in restoring its image and reputation. It examines what is needed to be done for an organization to rebuild the lost trust. Several crisis cases will be used to investigate this topic. The students will explore on what constitutes a good post-crisis communication in this post-modern era.

Key concepts: post-crisis communication

Week 11 Guest speaker

An expert in crisis communication and management will be invited to give a talk to students.

Week 12 and 13 Corporate social responsibility, sustainability and crisis

The concept of corporate social responsibility (CSR) will be introduced. Cases showing the increased public demand on corporate social responsibility will be presented. The evolution of the concepts of CSR will also be discussed. The class will then examine the relationship between corporate social responsibility and pre-crisis, crisis and post-crisis management.

Key concepts: corporate social responsibility, business ethics

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Advertising and Society
courses.description:
(UGEC2638 is double-coded with COMM2840.)

In this course, students will analyze real life campaigns to understand major effects of advertising in everyday life. Students will examine topics like materialism and commercialization of friendship to see how advertising persuade consumers through subtle uses of messages. They will also decode the formation and shifting of values promoted by Government and green campaigns. The course will help students distinguish between authentic and mediated reality regarding topics on artificial perfection of body image, sexual objectification and gender stereotyping.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2638 is double-coded with COMM2840. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM2840. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *At the end of** **this course, students will:**

1. Identify the multifaceted effects of mass-mediated advertising messages along the dimensions of subliminal messaging, infusion of constructed meanings, and mediation of reality.

2. Recognize the impacts of advertising on personal and psychological development.

3. Critically analyze advertising messages and motivations.

4. Investigate beyond the seemingly superficial phenomenon created by advertising into deeper issues related to living attitude and social values.

5. Develop a curiosity towards real life campaigns that promote meaningful causes that benefit citizens in Hong Kong.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *I. SUBLIMINAL PERSUASION**

* *Week** **1****: Subliminal Messaging and** **Materialism**

This week will introduce briefly all three sections and emphasis more specifically on subliminal persuasion, using materialism, luxury branding in China as examples. China has replaced Japan as the second strongest economic power in the world in 2012. It has also surpassed the US to become the second largest luxury brand market in 2009, spending of $9.4 billion and accounting for 27.5% of total global sales of luxury brands in the world. The invasion of luxury brands will inevitably alter the spending culture in China. Luxury brand ads hint subtly that consumers using them belong to a higher social group in the society. Students will discuss the subliminal indicators of luxury brand ads and their effects on attitudes towards social status in the society.

* *Week** **2****: Commercialization of Friendship in Social Networking Sites**

Social networking sites are dominating the media landscape among young people. Many viral ads are circulated through the disguise of sincere recommendations from friends, who actually share information for an incentive. This class will look into the core of this issue: should friendship be commercialized for personal gains?

* *Week 3: Properties, Personal Loan Ads and Wealth**

The recent waves of glamorized Hong Kong properties ads disseminated in China led to grave consequences in raising the prices of flats in Hong Kong. The property ads In Hong Kong shape unrealistic desires in viewers to own a flat that demands a lifetime of hard earned salaries. Personal loan ads encourage a supposedly free life of spending with no responsibility. This lesson will discuss the dynamics of these subliminal messages in affecting one’s decision about how to spend his / her money.

* *Week** **4****: Political Campaigns and Elections**

The presence of political campaigns in commercial media becomes prevalent these days due to the rise of democratization in the election process. This lesson will look into the various tactics and subliminal strategies used and manipulated in political advertising and its effects on public participation in election.

* *II. MEDIATION OF REALITY**

* *Week** **5****: Beauty Ads and Body Image**

This lesson will start with an in-depth look at the concept of mediation of reality, using studies conducted in Hong Kong that relate beauty and slimming product / service ads to a negative self-perceived body image in both men and women. Teenagers, in particular, are finding their self in their growing years by comparing themselves to the models in the ads. The gap between the idealized self and actual self creates frustrations among many. To bridge the gap, some fall for crash diets and some for desperate acts of plastic surgeries.

* *Week** **6****: Stereotypical Sex Ads and Gender Roles**

This lesson looks into the relationship between commoditization and objectification of the body and the resultant stereotypical roles played by men and women. Students will be challenged to live beyond the fixed roles narrowly defined and presented in the pseudo-reality.

* *Week** **7****: Tutor King / Queen Ads and Education**

The educational system in Hong Kong requires students to acquire incessant training and upgrading. Many tutors chanced this opportunity to create fast track learning to success by advertising their success rate of getting a student to obtain an As. This form of promotion alters students’ mentality to learning. Tutors acting as opinion leaders in ads create a trend of commercialized education.

* *Week** **8**: **A “Copycat” Culture**

“Copycat” China refers not only to the many cases of copying of products but also the imitation of ideas and other intellectual properties in China. Advertising is an industry that is keen on creativity, the very core element that sustains the industry. Piracy will suffocate the creative industry in the long run. Students will scan the creative landscape in China and learn to identify the seemingly original creative reality.

* *III. INFUSION OF CONSTRUCTED MEANINGS**

* *Week** **9****: Freedom of Speech and the Press**

This class will start examining the idea about meaning and value driven advertising/ advocacy. Recent cases show that advertising is affecting the press in Hong Kong and the Mainland has been censoring a lot of ads online and outdoor. What is the value of commercial speech? How much would the commercial speech be compromised? Will the censorship erode creativity, global branding strategy and business development? Students will investigate the longstanding struggle of the protection of speech in Hong Kong and the mainland.

* *Week** **10****: Globalizing and Standardization**

Global brands launched by global advertising agencies bring about their unique culture from the country-of-origin into a foreign country. For a global brand to be successfully adopted by local citizens, the agencies need to accommodate the traditional culture. However, the global influence for standardization sometimes surpasses localization, resulting in a pervasive infusion of foreign values. The balance and consideration of both cultures are the center of discussion in this lesson. A few global campaigns around the world will be presented to demonstrate the delicate balance between globalization and localization.

* *Week 11: “Anti” Campaigns and Social Movements**

This lesson will look into the value-driven impact and of Public Service Announcements (PSAs), including the anti-smoking, anti-drug and anti-AIDS campaigns on society. The lesson will also focus on the development, planning and execution of those campaigns. It is the purpose of the lesson to raise the awareness of the students in these cause advertising campaigns.

* *Week 12: Earth Hour, Outdoor Light Pollution and other Green Campaigns**

Greenpeace and other environmental protection groups have been working on major campaigns to improve the living conditions of the world. A few successful green campaigns will be discussed in class to reveal their value shifting strategies.

* *Week 1****3****: Food, Drug Ads and Public Health**

World Health Organization has established the strong tie between advertising of high fat, salt and sugar (HFSS) food and obesity. While UK has exercised blanket ban of food advertising to children and many other countries following suit, the Broadcasting Authority in Hong Kong has only advised five cases in the past four years regarding HFSS food ads to children. This lesson will investigate the difficult path to policy change in the business sector in Hong Kong. Advertising of all medicinal products in Hong Kong is strictly controlled by the Undesirable Medical Advertisements Ordinance (Cap 231) (the UMAO). Section 3 of the UMAO provides for an outright prohibition against the publication of 'any advertisement likely to lead to the use of any medicine … for the purpose of treating … or preventing' any disease, disorder or abnormal physical state. However, some prominent direct-to-consumer prescription drug ads are produced and broadcasted in Hong Kong recently. DTC drug advertising will change the traditional beliefs towards doctor-patient relationship and the demand of name-brand drugs at the expense of generic or equally effective drugs. Students will explore the Campaigns of Gardasil and Cervarix to find out their use of Government bodies as façade to lure the public to consult doctors about the drugs.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Indian Cultures and Society
courses.description:
(UGEC2655 is double-coded with ANTH2324.)
This course is an anthropological introduction to contemporary India, its social life and diverse cultures. India is home to more than a billion people, who look differently, speak various languages, practice different religions, and have distinct rituals, cuisines, and music. It is one of the world’s powers with global economic, political, and intellectual influence. Moreover, it shares important ties in the sphere of philosophy, religion, and medicine with China and other Asian societies. Therefore, students will learn about India’s place both in the world and the Asian region, including its ties with Hong Kong. Students will also develop an understanding of the country’s diversity and complex social phenomena such as kinship, communalism, caste system, tribe, third gender, and class. We will discuss pressing issues and theoretical debates related to globalization, sexuality, social movements, religious conflicts, public health, environment, and labor, and how these issues have been shaped by post-colonial politics and current transnational processes.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2655 is double-coded with ANTH2324. 
Not for Anthropology Majors; and students who have taken ANTH2324 or 3324. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to do the following:

* understand and analyze the diversity of Indian society in terms of region, caste, class, religion, language, gender, and other sociocultural divisions

* identify and compare the main ideas of various schools of philosophy and religion that originated in the Indian subcontinent

* describe and give examples of the everyday life of Indian women and men, as well as hijras, and other persons who identify differently

* explain the impact of India’s colonial history on its modern society

* examine the role of popular culture, political processes, and the global economy in the lives of Indians in India and abroad

* explain the cultural influences of India on the Asian region and the world

* critically assess the academic literature, news, and public discourses about various aspects of the Indian society
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Indian population in terms of linguistic, cultural, and regional diversity;**

Indo-European and Dravidian languages as the major linguistic groups in India; Differences between South and North India, special positions of the North East, Kashmir, and the Andaman islands

* *Caste system (*varna*, *jati*), Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (indigenous groups)**

The division of the Indian society into castes and those considered to be outside the caste system. History and contemporary practices related to caste discrimination and privilege; the place of the indigenous groups known as tribals or *Adivasi*

* **hijra*** **(third gender)**

Communities of people who identify neither men nor women

* *India’s independence, Partition (of India and Pakistan)**

The significance of 1947 Indian independence from the British colonial rule, the establishment of India and Pakistan, and its impact on present-day India

* *Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Jainism, religious festivals (*Diwali*, *oli*)**

Different religions as well as their rituals, beliefs, festivals, political representations, and family practices

* *Arranged marriage, extended family, modern femininities and masculinities**

The significance of family relations and arranged marriages in India; different models of being a woman and being a man in India, specifically Indians imagine themselves as “traditional” or “modern” women and men

* *Yoga, Ayurveda, Indian sports and medicine**

History and contemporary practices of Indian health traditions of Yoga and Ayurveda; how Indians take care of their health and body, different sports they play

* *Curry and other Indian foods**

Regional differences in foods; the impact of colonial history on contemporary habits and preferences in eating, cooking and dining

* *Bollywood and Indian popular culture**

The cultural, economic, and political importance of the Bollywood industry; other regional film industries in India

* *Migration, Indians in Hong Kong**

Indian diasporas around the world; the history and current processes of migration of Indians to Hong Kong; the experiences of locally born Indians in Hong Kong

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Ethnographies of Japan
courses.description:
(UGEC2657 is double-coded with ANTH2327.)
This course provides an introduction to contemporary Japanese society and culture. In the popular imagination, Japan occupies a complex and often contradictory position. It is home to futuristic anime and an aging population, picturesque villages and dolphin hunts, high-end cameras and the widespread use of quaint fax machines. Engaging with anthropological literature, students will learn to analyze, discuss, and write about various issues and cultural features of Japan, including youth, popular culture, self, family, labor, medicine, and health. An overarching theme will be how Japanese culture and society is changing in the transition to a highly aged society. We will examine persistent cultural patterns as well as the emergence of new forms of social life as residents of Japan grapple with smaller families, precarity, migration, and a rising population of older people. Students will learn how to apply theoretical concepts from anthropology and think critically about Japanese culture and its portrayals in the media. The ethnographic approaches and theoretical perspectives covered in this class will be applicable to other cultural contexts. Since Hong Kong, China, and Korea are following Japan’s path of population aging, this course provides an opportunity to explore cultural issues that have a local and regional significance.

courses.learning_outcomes:
* Students will acquire a robust knowledge of contemporary Japanese society and culture. They will develop an understanding of cultural diversity within Japan and the broad shifts associated with population aging.

* Students will gain the ability to apply anthropological theory to analyze Japanese society and culture. In conjunction, students will learn to critically evaluate scholarly and media portrayals of Japan. These critical faculties will also be relevant for understanding their own or other societies in daily life as well as for future anthropological studies.

* Students will develop their writing skills. In addition to conventional academic essays, students will learn to write ethnographically about a specific site. Through writing, students will gain skills in communication of their own observations and perspectives on cultural features. These skills can be used for further academic study as well as personal and professional life.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part I: Foundations of Japanese Culture and Society

Week 1. What is Japanese culture?

* This lesson introduces the concept of culture and gives a brief history on the sociocultural and geographical boundaries of Japan.

Week 2. Foundational Works

* This lesson provides students with an introduction to early major writings about Japan, including early European and American visitors to Japan.

Week 3. Myths of Japaneseness

* This session will examine of common media tropes about Japan and the pseudo-scholarly genre of writing known as *Nihonnjinron*. It explores forms of ethnocentricism, conceptions of cultural uniqueness, and nationalism in post WWII Japan.

Week 4. Traditions and Inventions

* This session focuses on the ways that traditions created and how people use them to give meaning to life. Through a discussion of *bushido*, the class will illuminate the recent invention of traditions popularly considered ancient and timeless in Japan.

Week 5. Health and the Body

* The session provides a conceptual overview of how people in Japan understand their bodies, health, and illness. Particular attention will be paid to longevity and issues involved in aging.

Week 6. Gift-giving and Ritual

* An exploration of situational, lifecycle, and calendar-based gift-giving and ritual in contemporary Japan.

II. The Life Cycle in an Aging Japan

Week 7. Love, Marriage, and Children

* This session provides an overview of romantic relationships, including non-heteronormative relationships, and reasons for low fertility in Japan. Romance in late life will also be part of the discussion.

Week 8. Childhood and Schooling

* Focusing on preschool through high school, this session examines the ways children are taught to become adults in Japanese society.

Week 9. Cute and *Otaku*

* This class explores the origins of subcultures in Japan and how they are co-opted by the state and companies. It will highlight the ways that young people’s participation in these subcultures receives blame for low fertility.

Week 10. Labor, Precarity, and Class

* This session is an examination of the changes in Japanese labor following WWII in relation to security, gender, and socioeconomic class. It will highlight how precarious working conditions lead individuals to delay or avoid marriage and having children.

Week 11. Gender

* Students will learn about how gender intersects with family, work, and social roles. This session will highlight conventional roles of the male “salaryman” and the housewife, paying attention to female caregiving for older family members.

Week 12. Aging and the End of Life

* This session examines the experiences of late life ideals for death .

Week 13. Atomic Radiation and the Plight of Older People after Fukushima

* A broad discussion of Japan complicated relationship with radioactive decay, including atomics bombs, Godzilla, and the meltdown in Fukushima. Particular attention will be paid to case of aging survivors of the atomic bombs and older people’s communities displaced after the disasters following the earthquake on 11.3.2011.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Culture and Business
courses.description:
(UGEC2662 is double-coded with ANTH2510.)

Culture is ubiquitous in every aspect of societies, including how we do business. This course will examine the role of culture in contemporary business and study work and management in industrial societies anthropologically. Students will be introduced to the cultural logics of business practices, particularly business operations, organization and management through ethnographic explorations of different cultures, locales and sociohistorical settings. The aims of the course are twofold. First, it reveals cultural aspects and the cultural mechanisms of business. It shows the significance of culture in the business world, as well as the cultural significance of business. Second, it attempts to put anthropology into business practice. It demonstrates to students how anthropological knowledge and methodologies can be applied to business operations and help to achieve business goals. By examining the themes including but not limited to the indoctrination of work ethics, labor relations, gender and racial issues in the workplace, capitalism and its discontents, and responses to and actions upon market capitalism in terms of both production and consumption, the course attends to these Sustainable Development Goals: No Poverty (SDG#1), Gender Equality (SDG#5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG#8), Reduced Inequalities (SDG#10), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG#12), and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG#17).

courses.course_syllabus:
The course is structured in three parts. *Part I Culture in Business* explores the cultural dimensions of workplaces and corporate management. We begin with an overview of the temporal and spatial reconfigurations since industrialization in order to discern modern work ethics, followed by explorations of dynamics in the workplace. Next, we will explore discourses in shaping corporate operations and management, and consider (and challenge) the ideas of economization, maximization, auditing and accountability. This part decodes life in business settings, and practices in corporations. *Part II Business Ventures in the Globalizing World* situates the discussions in current trends of capitalism. We will look into what makes us buy and spend, and how traditional values and modern business practices mingle. It raises the question of whether we are really emancipated under the fashion of decentralization by exploring the gig economy and the phenomenon of self-enterprising. We will also examine how we can build a more inclusive, diverse and equal society by finding a new way out from the existing business ideologies and practices. *Part III Anthropology and the Business World* discusses how to apply anthropology in business settings, looking into how and why anthropology and anthropologists are important to the private sector, and broadly speaking, to the modern capitalist world. The course concludes by contemplating whether business is really business.

Overall, through the examinations of how we are taught to work, produce, and buy, the imperative of gender and racial stereotypes in the workplace, turns in capitalism and the rise of new economies and the pertinent social and cultural phenomena, the course addresses the following Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): No Poverty (SDG#1), Gender Equality (SDG#5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG#8), Reduced Inequalities (SDG#10), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG#12), and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG#17).

* *Core topics:**

Week 1 Course Introduction

Week 2 Seeing Business Anthropologically **(SDGs 17)**

* *Part I Culture in Business**

Week 3 Space, Time and Work Ethics **(SDGs 8, 10)**

Week 4 Gender, Race/Ethnicity, and Communication in the Workplace **(SDGs 5, 8, 10)**

Week 5 Corporatization, Economization and Maximization **(SDGs 1, 8, 10, 12)**

Week 6 Audit Culture and Accountability **(SDGs 8)**

Week 7 Mid-term Test

* *Part II Business Ventures in the Globalizing World**

Week 8 The Making of Consumers **(SDGs 10, 12)**

Week 9 Fieldtrip to a Social Enterprise/ a Social Innovation Project/ an exhibition about reindustrialization in Hong Kong

Week 10 The Gig Economy and Self-enterprising **(SDGs 1, 8, 10)**

Week 11 Ethical-Political Consumerism and Social Entrepreneurialism **(SDGs 1, 5, 8, 10, 12, 17)**

* *Part III Anthropology and the Business World**

Week 12 Applying Anthropology to Business Practice **(SDGs 10, 17)**

Week 13 Conclusion: Is Business Really Business?

courses.title: Sports and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2664 is double-coded with ANTH2390.)

This course will examine the role and importance of sports in different societies and cultures, in the present and the past. Sports are often thought of as trivial, or as unimportant games to amuse young people. But in the wealthiest countries, sports represent huge portions of GDP and are important topics of daily conversation. Almost half the world watched the 2010 football/soccer World Cup. Sports have been compared to religions in their ability to unite people and to inspire fanatical devotion.

The academic study of sports is interdisciplinary, with contributions from psychologists, historians, gender studies scholars, sociologists and anthropologists. This course will take an interdisciplinary approach while emphasizing anthropology’s focus on culture, on the experience of participants, and on both symbolic and political-economy aspects of sports. Topics will include Race and Performance, Sports and Rituals, Sports as Moral Education, Gender and Sexuality in Sport, Sports and Nationalism, Globalization of Sport, the Olympics, and Sports Stars and the Media. Students will be expected to do a research project for the course.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Social Media and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2665 is double-coded with ANTH2540.)

This course addresses the ways in which social media and other related interactions in cyberspace have become a central element in the everyday lives of humans across the globe in the 21st Century. Our modern lives are now largely interwoven with digital technologies that have not only changed our own cultures, but also have brought forth new cultural forms through mobile phone technologies, networked “smart”-products, and cultural groupings only possible through digital means. The course approaches the anthropology of these digital cultures through its main themes—the transformation and expansion of social media, social research online, the intermixing of our online and offline lives, critical social issues of online lives, and the question of posthumanism. These themes are addressed explicitly in the course, and are also the subtexts of the different lectures, readings, and project work. Students will learn the techniques of online fieldwork and referencing. They will explore a diverse array of new ethnographies on social media: on gender, political movements, online dating, hacking, and gaming culture. These ethnographies also serve to model online social research and provide examples of methodology and design. The social consequences of cyberspace are addressed in the topics of internet pornography, addiction, surveillance, activism, and social networking. Gender and identity issues are a continuous theme throughout the course, highlighting how online lives accentuate already existing dynamics. Hong Kong connections to these subjects will also be critically discussed, often drawing on topical themes presented on blogs and forums. Students will learn of the philosophical questions of posthumanism and the nature of technologically mediated human culture. This serves as a philosophical ballast to the course allowing students to reflect personally on their own experiences and how technology has and will continue to shape their lives. The role of anthropology in understanding and capturing human culture in this context anchors on the investigation of how technology is possibly making us ‘more’ human than previous forms of cultural life.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2665 is double-coded with ANTH2540. 
Not for Anthropology Majors; and students who have taken ANTH2540. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
* After taking this course students will have learnt how to design and perform online fieldwork and manage digital referencing.

* Students will know of and understand the recent history and development of the internet and key platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, eBay, iTunes, and the ways in which cyberspace has become embedded in the everyday work and social lives of over 2.4 billion internet users.

* Students will be able to explain and discuss the various debates on the social consequences of online technologies with regard to the tensions between online lives and (so called) real lives, or digital dualism.

* Students will be able to address and articulate issues of political and philosophical change, activism, addiction, surveillance, the body and visual culture in connection to mobile technologies.

* Students will know of some philosophical discussions on the nature of humanity in this new epoch. The question of humanity, posthuman futures, and transhumanism is a key concern that runs throughout the course. Students will also come to consider social media and our changing digital cultures as deeply significant to new understandings of gender and body identity.
courses.course_syllabus:
Core Content

1. **Online Field Work** – Exploring how researchers have performed social research online. This will equip students with a knowledge of the approaches, techniques and challenges of field work in cyberspace. Whilst being a core topic, this is also part of the weekly project work of the course. Students will start their digital research from the beginning of the course, by first developing a blog and networking with classmates.
2. **Cultural History of Cyberspace** – How did the world go online? This topic addresses the historical and technological developments that led the world to go online. Its key concern is to highlight how this has altered and affected society, and how quickly online life has become a part of everyday life.
3. **Social Networking Sites** – The rise of web 2.0 and how the internet has become social. How have different SNS emerged, how do they connect, isolate, liberate, and limit social activity? Online Culture is explored via the different uses of various SNS platforms, and their own identities.
4. **Sex and Body Culture in Cyberspace** – Tackles the social consequences of online pornography in different social and cultural circumstances. Body politics, risk, and sexuality online.
5. **Posthumanism** – This is framed in the first week as a key issue and returns as the focus of the last 2 weeks of the course.This topic looks at the impact of cyberspace on our philosophical understanding of our bodies and ourselves. How is technology changing our attitudes to gender, ethnicity, religion, and is it making us more or less human?
6. **Online Activism** – Explores the relationship between cyberspace and participatory politics, social justice, terror, and extremist groups

Proposed weekly topics with core content highlighted.

Week 1:- Introduction: Starting Digital Research (Going Viral)

Week 2:- Cultural History of Cyberspace

Week 3:- Social Networking Sites

Week 4:- Sex and Body Culture in Cyberspace

Week 5:- Video Gaming Culture – Play & Recreation

Week 6 :- Internet Addiction

Week 7:- Online Activism

Week 8:- Cyber-Surveillance and Crime

Week 9:- Online Field Work

Week 10:- Free Software, Inclusion, and Sharing

Week 11:- Virtual, Real, and Hybrid Space

Week 12:- The Selfie, the Self and Posthumanism

Week 13:- Future Scenarios of Cyberspace

* *Thematics:**

* *Online Research** is covered as part of project work throughout the course. Weekly work on blogs relate to class discussions and require students to source and reference. It is addressed as a key topic in Week 1 & Week 9.

* *Social Consequences** of online lives as a theme is most strongly represented in the topics of week 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11. As well, because of the salience of this topic it relates to other core topics such as 3,4,7, 11, and 12.

* *Posthumanism** is a philosophical theme that is introduced in Week 1 and is relevant throughout the course. It is tackled directly as a concluding theme in the final two weeks of the course (12 and 13).

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Interpersonal Violence
courses.description:
(UGEC2680 is double-coded with SOWK2200.)

The purposes of this course are to provide students a basic understanding of violence that takes place in our daily life in the contexts of intimate relationship, family, school and community and to arouse their consciousness of contemporary values of equality, human rights and social justice. Various concepts and theories of violence will be introduced to explore the nature, causes, consequences and trends of violence in different aspects of life. Emphasis will be placed on the issues of interpersonal violence in contemporary societies. Social policy and provisions to prevent and eliminate interpersonal violence will also be discussed.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2680 is double-coded with SOWK2200. 
Not for Social Work Majors; and students who have taken SOWK2200.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:

1. Critically examine the contemporary perspectives, concepts and theories on interpersonal violence.

2. Analyze causes and consequences of interpersonal violence in different contexts.

3. Apply and integrate interdisciplinary theories of violence to evaluate current policy and strategies on tackling violence.

4. Reflect on ways to combat violence and help to promote a peaceful environment.

5. Appreciate the contemporary values of equality, human rights and social justice.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Common misunderstanding and myths of interpersonal violence.

2. Contemporary perspectives and theories of violence from anthropology, education, medical science, politics, psychology, sociology and social work.

3. Nature, causes, consequences and trends of interpersonal violence.

4. The needs of victims and perpetrators of interpersonal violence.

5. Risk and protective factors of violence at personal, family, school, community and policy levels.

6. Issues of violence in regard to different genders, ages, classes, sexual orientations and cultures.

7. Current social policy and prevention programs on interpersonal violence.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Social Innovation and Social Change for Good
courses.description:
(UGEC2686 is double-coded with SOWK2204.)

This course prepares students to learn from the emerging practices of social innovations in tackling with challenges in social, economic, cultural and political development in Hong Kong, the Greater China region and beyond. Students will acquire analysis, knowledge and strategies of social innovations, the processes of social change in creating social values. The scope of social innovations includes that of social entrepreneurs or social innovators in NGOs, communities, social movements, non-profit organizations, and business as well as the public sector. The course will examine cases of social innovations that have catalyzed important positive social change through the market, the nonprofit sector, the community, the public sector as well as the spaces among those four sectors.

Experiential learning will be integrated along the course delivery, such as programmme visits, dialogue with social entrepreneurs, staff members or service users. Students are encouraged to experience these operations, so as to analyze the development issues, the social values and innovations in offering practical solutions to poverty and social inequalities, unemployment and livelihood, civic and community engagement, fair trade as well as sustainable development. The course will provide inspirations as well as know-hows for students who are concerned about the articulation of local with global and regional issues and like to develop innovative actions to change the society for good.

courses.description:
(UGEC2693 is double-coded with SOWK2203.)

This course introduces to students the field of mission-driven social enterprise, which aims to achieve a balance between meaningful social returns as well as sustainable or competitive financial returns through their products, services and other business practices. Through examining the best practices in social entrepreneurship, it also stimulates students to explore how social enterprise can affect policy and facilitate system change. Experiential learning elements such as visiting social enterprises and having dialogue with social entrepreneurs, staff members or service users will be arranged in order to let students experience its operation, understand its practice as well as to enable students in realizing its possibilities in offering solutions to education, healthcare, environment, workforce development, international development and other societal issues. The course is valuable to students who may want to design or lead a mission-driven social enterprise, or want to contribute time and energy to help build the social sector through this emerging field.

courses.description:
(UGEC2710 is double-coded with EDUC2130.)

The course is aimed at preparing students as global and future citizens who not only have critical understandings of the environmental issues, but also the capabilities and attitudes to take an active role in tackling the issues and educating for the environment. This course is structured around key issues pertaining to environmentalism and environmental education, including climate changes, sustainability, green groups and environmental curriculum and teaching at schools. Using an issue-inquiry approach, course participants will be led to critically reflect on the issues from various perspectives: philosophical, scientific, social and educational. The different approaches to environmental education in the Western and Chinese communities will be explored in the contexts of eastern and western cultures. A field trip is included to provide experiential education in the environment.

3. Is climate change a myth or hoax - understanding the science behind and its limitations

4. Why don’t people take climate change seriously - consequences and solutions of climate change

5. What’s wrong with the countries – politics and the environment

6. What’s wrong with our society – modern capitalism and the environment

7. Is sustainable development a myth?

8. What’s wrong with human beings – environmental ethics?

9. What’s wrong with the environmental advocacy groups - myths of some environmental activities?

10. What's wrong with our education - aims and approaches of environmental education?

11. How do different countries approach environmental education –Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and others

12. Overview of issues related to environmental problems and environmental education

13. Field trip to a site related to current environmental issues in Hong Kong, such as North East development farmland, EcoPark, Fung Yuen butterfly convervation centre.

courses.course_syllabus:
講授內容

（一）中醫的概念﹕中醫、中藥與中國文化

概括介紹中國醫學的起源、形成、發展、學術特點及與中國傳統文化的密切關係，討論嶺南中醫藥文化以及中西醫的比較。

（二）中醫藥與儒、釋、道家文化以及《易經》的關係

簡述中醫藥文化與儒、釋、道三家以及易經的關係：儒家的仁、禮、中庸之道與中醫藥環環相扣，相互參照；釋家「醫方明」與中醫理論相互吸收和影響；道家學說不少與中醫理論類通，同樣強調人與大自然的關係和天人相應；

《黃帝內經》對自然和人體的認識，及其辨證理論，一脈相承自《易經》。

（三）文學與中醫

以儒通醫。古代學者如陶潛、陸游、蘇軾、羅貫中、曹雪芹等都曾經行醫或有深厚的中醫造詣。 中醫不少著作是用詩、詞、歌、賦形式撰寫的，讀者容易記憶，文學著作亦有豐富的中醫內容。本節選讀唐詩、宋詞、紅樓夢、三國演義等文學著作，欣賞其中包含的中醫宇宙觀、生命觀、並討論其中所列舉的藥物，病案。

（四）中醫理論之應用﹕飲食、養生之中醫文化

從簡介舌診、臟腑辨證、君臣佐使組方原理，先讓學生認識中醫診治方法，再以飲食和養生兩方面闡述中華寶庫之一----中醫保健之道。食療：飲食養生，家居實用補藥，涼茶及保健湯水。養生：四季養生法，十二時辰養生法，休憩養生與七情養生。保健、養顏：按摩、穴位和藥膳。

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Sexuality and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2853 is double-coded with GDRS2002.)

This course aims at an interdisciplinary approach to the study of human sexuality and culture. Three main areas will be discussed: (1) ideas of sexuality: Chinese and Western conception of sexuality, modern theories of sexuality; (2) sexuality and ethics: ethical issues of sexual relationships; and (3) sexuality and society: gender problem; issues relating to homosexuality, pornography, and AIDS.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2853 is double-coded with GDRS2002. 
Not for Philosophy Majors; and students who have taken GDRS2002. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Identify and recognize the ideas of sex and sexuality in Western and Chinese culture.

2. Discuss sexual issues openly and intellectually without any taboo.

3. Identify and reflect on various media representations of sex.

4. Appreciate the complexity of sexuality in modern society regarding homosexuality, feminism, etc.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. 導論：性、性事與文化（Sex, Sexuality and Culture）

2. 性事的思想

2. 1西方傳統性事理論

2. 2中國傳統色情思想

2. 3現代性事思想革命及其發展

3. 性事的表象

3. 1裸體／性事藝術之演變

3. 2身體 ／性器官之文化意義

3. 3性事與文字：色情書

3. 4性事與電影：藝術與淫褻之間

4. 性事的制度

4. 1性、愛與婚姻

4. 2「同性愛」

4. 3性別、性別主義與女性主義

5. 結論: 性事之意義

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Economic Reform and Social Impacts in China
courses.description:
(UGEC2883 is double-coded with SOCI2106.)

Focusing on economic reforms, students will be taught the impetus of the institutional changes in China and how they affect the cultural, socioeconomic and organizational lives of Chinese people. Key social science concepts and theories like institution, ideology, socialism, marketization, social control, civil society, industrialization, urbanization, stratification, family, socialization, and specialized terms in China studies like guanxi (關係), danwei (單位), hukou (戶口), harmonious society, China dream, floating population, rural-urban divide, one/two child(ren) policy, will be introduced and discussed from an integrated perspective. After taking this course, students should be able to grasp the transformation and development in key areas of China, including economic reform, political system and change, rural and urban development, social inequality, family and marriage, cultural and ideological issues, as well as other institutional developments.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2883 is double-coded with SOCI2106.
Not for Sociology Majors; and students who have taken GESC2118, SOCI2106 or UGEA2190.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Students are expected to grasp the basic knowledge about China’s major social institutions such as socialist market economy, party-state apparatus, stratification system, and lineage values. They should also be able to understand the evolution of these institutions over the past several decades.

• Students should be able to understand how social scientists analyze and examine the formation, evolution, and influences of the major social institutions in contemporary China. They are expected to grasp the key concepts and theories developed from social scientists from sociology, economics, political science, etc.

• Besides basic facts and social science perspectives, students are encouraged to critically evaluate some controversial topics from different angles through writing assignments. The topics will include key dilemmas in contemporary China regarding economic growth and social equality, state capacity and democracy, traditional culture and modernization, etc.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1: Introduction: Basic Information of the Chinese Society**

\* Provide basic information about the socio-economic characteristics of the contemporary China.

* *Week 2 & 3: China before Reform Era**

\* Provide information about the political systems, economic institutions, and social control mechanisms of China during Mao’s era.

* *Week 4** **& 5: Economic Reform**

\* Provide information about the processes of economic reform since 1978, as well as its impact on the economic system afterwards.

* *Week 6 & 7 & 8:** **Impacts on the Political System and the Preservation of the Party-state**

\* Provide information about the impact of the economic reform on the political system in China afterwards. Also, we will discuss the puzzle regarding the preservation of the Party-state despite the massive political reform.

* *Week 9****: Impacts on Rural-urban Development and Migration**

\* Provide information about the differential impact of the economic reform on the urban and rural development, as well as the resultant great migration since then.

* *Week 10: Impacts on Social Stratification and Inequality**

\* Provide information about the impact of the economic reform on the transition of the social stratification system and the enlarging social inequality.

* *Week 11 & 12: Impacts on Social Conflicts, Civil Society, and Social Control**

\* Provide information about the impact of the economic reform on the growing social conflicts and the newly emerged social control mechanisms.

* *Week 13: Impacts on Population and Demographic Transition**

\* Provide information about the impact of the economic reform on the population and demographic patterns.

* *[\*whether covering this depending on our schedule, because we may save some time for students to finish the final paper before the due date\*]**

meetings.location: Lee Shau Kee Archi Bldg G02

courses.description: When money is fiat, land is scarce, housing becomes a good hedge of inflation. However, when housing is both an investment capital as well as a necessity, the city is split into an owner-renter dichotomy, with the former preferring an increase of housing prices but just the opposite for the latter. When the pendulum of housing price swings to one side, housing capital can result in negative equity, asset bubble, or even financial crisis. Swinging to the other end, housing can become unaffordable, even if public housing or subsidy can be provided. Decent living environment and sustainable community are the concerns of cities. This introduction course explores the reasons of the housing price fluctuations and the implications of the dichotomy on the city lives.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Urban Studies Majors. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.course_syllabus:
The following topics are included in the course:

PART I: Relationships between money, land and housing

1. Why housing can be a good hedge of inflation?
2. How does the monetary policy affect the housing market?
3. Why interest rate and inflation rate affect housing price?
4. Is high land price or restrictive land supply a cause of high housing price?
5. How does the housing policy affect the housing market?

PART II: Social implications of housing issues

1. What is the owner-renter dichotomy of housing?
2. What are the implications of the housing dichotomy on our city lives?
3. Why housing can become unaffordable?
4. How does housing price fluctuation affect financial stability and wealth inequality?
5. Why are there housing cycles and housing bubbles?
6. What is property hegemony?

PART III:

1. Is public housing or cooperative housing a solution?
2. A sustainable housing policy.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Belt and Road for Collaborative Modernization
courses.description:
(UGEC2917 is double-coded with URSP2010.)

The Belt and Road initiative (BRI) refers to the Silk Road Economic Belt and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. It is a significant development strategy proposed by the Chinese Government spanning approximately 60 countries in Asia, Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa, with a total population of 4.4 billion. This initiative takes advantage of global transportation routes, core cities, and key ports to build international economic co-operation corridors. The effective operation and management of the BRI require collaboration among a broad range of disciplines comprising civil engineering, material science, government operations, economics and finance, social and political science, and environmental science. A critical and multi-disciplinary understanding of the BRI can provide insights into basic requirements, geopolitical impact, physical barriers, and sustainability potential of the infrastructural projects it proposes to undertake and help relevant stakeholders address large-scale and complex challenges in the lifecycle management of those infrastructure projects. This course involves forward-looking perspectives to assess, predict, influence and enhance the in/direct network effects and benefits of the BRI on the cities, urban systems and peoples of the Belt and Road region.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2917 is double-coded with URSP2010. 
Not for Urban Studies Majors; and students who have taken URSP2010.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.course_syllabus:
Introduction

1. Globalization in Perspective: introduction of globalization as a term, process and ideology.

2. Historical Silk Road: historical origins of the Silk Road; continuities and shifts in terms of Maritime Silk Road, interactions and encounters along the Silk Road.

Global Implications

3. Geopolitical Shifts: branding and popularizing the Belt and Road Initiative; imperial histories and ambitions informing the initiative.

4. Eastern and Western Perspectives: the opportunities and challenges arising from Belt and Road Initiative with reference to the European Recovery Program; the geopolitical theories of Alfred Mahan, Halford Mackinder and Henry Kissinger; the philosophy of Confucius and Taoists.

Facilities Connectivity

5. Construction Management in BRI countries: risk management in international construction joint ventures and overseas development institute; large-scale transnational high-speed railway construction projects.

6. Green and Sustainable Urbanization: In search of better livability in BRI cities: Liveability in dense and vertical cities; green finance; carbon auditing and carbon trading; green strategies for achieving sustainable development goals.

Unimpeded Trade

7. Trading, Logistic, and Professional Service: Hong Kong as regional BRI centre for trading, logistic and professional services; manufacture shifting and upgrading experience in ASEAN economies.

8. The Energy Market: energy market opportunities and uncertainties in Northeast, Southeast, Central Asia and Africa; global oil and gas markets; renewable and sustainable energy goals.

Financial Integration

9. The Bond Market: infrastructure financing; international bond market and Hong Kong’s debt market; corporate social responsibility on Green Bond Issuance; the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the Silk Road Fund.

10. International Settlement: currency wars and special drawing rights; consumerism and RMB internationalization; Hong Kong as the offshore RMB centre; the New Development Bank.

Regional Responses

11. Middle East: geopolitics and energy nexus; religious and national concerns.

12. Central and Eastern Europe: rail and maritime connectivities; integrating trade and resisting xenophobia.

13. India: regional rivalry, economic integration and border disputes

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Language and Society
courses.description:
(UGEC2925 is double-coded with LING2301.)
This course explores human language in the broader context of culture and society. How, for example, does one language community interacts with another language community in the multilingual world? Does language change and what are the processes involved? To what extent does the same language vary due to gender, power, status, and identity? How do men and women, people with higher and lower social status talk differently? How are these relationships reflected in the use of politeness markers and other linguistic devices? What are the implications of sociolinguistics on education and language planning?

Through introducing students to major issues in sociolinguistic studies, students will be able to develop a better understanding of how language functions in societal contexts from a linguistic perspective. Discussions will also focus on common sociolinguistic phenomena in daily communication, with a specific emphasis on the use of various languages and dialects spoken in Hong Kong. Exploring these topics will enhance students’ awareness of language as a cultural phenomenon and sharpen their sensitivity to the nuances of language use in the context of a multilingual world, with special reference to the sociolinguistic context of the Greater China area.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2925 is double-coded with LING2301.

courses.course_syllabus:
Languages, dialects and varieties

* Language vs. dialect, language standardization, regional dialects, social dialects, styles, registers and genres

Multilingual societies and discourse

* Multilingualism, diglossia, code-switching, language shift, maintenance, and revitalization

Contact languages

* Lingua francas, pidgin and creole formation, linguistic characteristics of pidgins and creoles

Language variation and change

* Regional variation, linguistic variables, social variation, gender variation, language change

Language, gender and sexuality

* Sexist language, gender and sexuality identities

Sociolinguistics and education

* Social dialects and education, multilingual education, English as a global language

Language attitudes and identity

* Language attitudes and effects on identity; how identities are expressed through variations of language

Language policy and planning

* The goals of language policies, the role of government and language users, the roles of ethnic and national identities
