courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Thinking sustainability: Health and Global Challenges
courses.description:
In this course, we will discuss the direct and indirect health consequences related to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by the United Nations and analyze the wider socioeconomic dimensions of these topics. After the pandemic we faced, we realized that a health crisis will have implications beyond the health sector and development must balance social, economic and environmental sustainability. It is therefore important for us, as global citizens, to recognize the issues related and understand how we can take part in this. Traditionally, health indicators have been an important aspect of development indices and health is a foundation of societies. Therefore, our course aims to discuss SDGs through the lens of health, by providing an overview on how the current global challenges on sustainable development impacts the population health and encourage students to look for solutions. We will cover the health-related SDGs by blended learning, including 2. Zero Hunger where we will discuss malnutrition, 3. Good Health and Well-being where we will discuss road injuries, infrastructure and management, 5. Gender Equality where we will discuss intimate partner violence, 6. Clean Water and Sanitation where we will discuss water safety and supply, 8. Decent Work and Economic Growth where we will discuss labor rights and occupational injuries, 11. Sustainable Cities and Communities where we will discuss impacts on health, socioeconomics and environment of inadequate housing and poor living environment, 13. Climate Action where we will discuss Climate-related disasters and disaster risks, and 16. Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions where we will discuss concept and impact of peace and justice on health.

Through face-to-face tutorials and case-based discussions, we will discuss selected topics in greater details, including the road safety aspects of Goal 3 “Good health and well-being”, the protection of workers from work-related injuries in Goal 8 “Decent work and economic growth”, the disaster risks in modern developments in Goal 13 “Climate action”, and how to educate the younger generation on the promotion of peace in Goal 16 “Peace, justice and strong institutions”. Development of modern societies and the interaction between humans and environment will be discussed, and through the advocacy framework we will discuss the current challenges related which draw immense global attention, and allow students to exchange interdisciplinary ideas, identify the challenges we are facing and propose advocacy campaign in hope to identify and deliver solutions locally and internationally.

- To gain knowledge on the direct and indirect health consequences of the selected SDG global challenges (SDG #2, #3, #5, #6, #8, #11, #13, #16)

- To analyze the wider socioeconomic dimensions of these challenges (SDG #2, #3, #5, #6, #8, #11, #13, #16)

- To appreciate the importance of good health in sustainable development and its positive impacts on economic growth and cultural development
courses.course_syllabus:
The course includes 8 online lectures introducing the 8 health-related SDGs and discussing related health issues with local and global data. Two SDG online lectures will be available on Blackboard every other week. The online lectures will start with SDG topics more related to personal health, ie. rights and equities. We will then move on to SDG topics related to the health of societies and health consequences related to the interaction between human development and nature. At the end, we will discuss SDG topics related to health issues that need to be address with global collaborations. The face-to-face tutorials will cover the 4 chosen SDGs, namely “Good health and well-being”, “Decent work and economic growth”, “Climate action” and “Peace, justice and strong institutions”, where we will have case studies and students will require the knowledge learnt in online lectures to participate in the discussions.

What role does compensation play in this important topic? * As climate change has increased the number of extreme hot days, what rights does outdoor workers (esp. construction workers) have in Hong Kong and internationally? |

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Museum and Heritage
courses.description: This course reviews the historical development of concepts and theories related to museums and cultural heritage. It introduces diversified definitions of museums and heritage in the contemporary. Through selected case studies and field trips, it demonstrates the operations of museums and heritage sites; and analyses their social roles in modern society. It aligns with the UN Sustainable Development Goals #11 'Sustainable Cities and Communities, which emphasises making more inclusive and sustainable cities and communities. It also reviews the historical evolution of international conventions related to museums and heritage outlines how global and regional cooperation, such as the development of UNESCO World Heritage, is vital for sustainable heritage conservation and management. It directly responds to the UN Sustainable Development Goals #17, 'Revitalise the Global Partnership for Sustainable Development which suggests that successful global development requires inclusive and international partnerships.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for History Majors; and students who have taken HIST3441. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.course_attributes:
SDG-GE #11 Sustainable Cities and Communities
SDG-GE #17 Partnerships for the Goals
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students should understand core concepts and theories related to museums and heritage in the contemporary world.
2. Students should learn about the historical evolution of social and cultural roles of museums and heritage, especially in the social context of the East Asian region. They shall further develop their capacity to review the social functions of museums and heritage in the rapidly changing contemporary society. It shall help students pinpoint the core values of the UN Sustainable Development Goals #11 'Sustainable Cities and Communities, which emphasises making more inclusive and sustainable cities and communities.
3. Students shall be able to outline the importance of international and regional cooperation on issues related to heritage conservation, such as the establishment of UNESCO and the *Modus Operandi* of the UNESCO World Heritage. It allows students to recognise the importance of global solidarity in achieving a successful and sustainable international development emphasised by the UN Sustainable Development Goals #17, 'Revitalise the Global Partnership for Sustainable Development.
courses.course_syllabus:
Section 1: Concepts and theories related to museums and heritage

1. The origin of the museum and its historical development.

2. The concepts and definitions of cultural heritage and their historical evolution.

3. Understanding and interpreting cultural heritage in the East Asian context.

Section 2: The social roles of museums and heritage and their public engagement

1. The transformation of the social roles of museums and heritage.

2. The educational functions of museums and heritage: how museums and heritage sites could collaborate to provide a culturally diversified learning experience for different society stakeholders, including children, the elderly, and people with physical and mental disabilities.

3. The social inclusion of museums and heritage: how museums and heritage could help motivate local societies' sustainable development and address the value of social justice worldwide.

4. The reuse and revitalisation of heritage in modern society.

Section 3: Achieving sustainable heritage conservation and management through International and regional cooperation

1. International conventions related to heritage conservation and management.

2. The *Modus Operandi* of UNESCO World heritage and its sustainable development goals.

3. The challenges and opportunities of international and regional cooperation regarding heritage conservation and management.

第一部：博物館及文化遺產的概念和理論

1. 博物館概念的源起、發展和擴充。

2. 文化遺產概念的源起及發展。

3. 東亞地區對於文化遺產概念的理解和演繹。

第二部：博物館及文化遺產的社會角色與公眾參與

1. 博物館及文化遺產社會角色的歷史演變。

2. 博物館和文化遺產的社會性教育功能：兩者如何共同協作為不同的社會群體例如兒童、長者和身心障礙人士提供文化多元和具包容性的學習體驗。

3. 博物館及文化遺產與不同社群公眾的關係和連結：兩者如何有助社區營造的過程以及確立社會公義的重要性。

4. 文化遺產在當代社會的活化和再利用。

第三部：國際及地區性合作與可持續的文化遺產管理

1. 有關文化遺產保育和管理的國際性公約和守則。

2. 聯合國世界文化遺產的運作及管理機制；以及其可持續發展目標。

3. 國際及地區性合作在文化遺產保育上所面對挑戰及機遇。

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: History of Hong Kong
courses.description: This course introduces the history of Hong Kong from a British colony to the Special Administrative Region of China. It covers major events and issues of Hong Kong, emphasizing the development of political system, social structure and economic pattern, and evaluate the role of Hong Kong in modern China, in the Asian-Pacific region and in the world. The course critically examines how colonial governance and Sino-British relations affected Hong Kong, offering students a multi-perspective in understanding how Hong Kong has becomes what it is today. This course is relevant to three Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly in the area of SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth by looking at the development of Hong Kong from an entrepôt to a global financial centre, SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities by looking at how Hong Kong evolved from a society of racial segregation to social inclusiveness, and SDG#16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions by looking at the public policy in promoting social reform and social justice.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for History Majors; and students who have taken GESC2150, GLBS3406. HIST2500 or UGEC3542.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.course_attributes:
SDG-GE #8 Decent Work and Economic Growth
SDG-GE #10 Reducing Inequality
SDG-GE #16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Have a better understanding on the history of Hong Kong.
2. Recognize and critically analyze how and why various contexts affecting the development of Hong Kong.
3. Identify and examine the economic roles and positions of Hong Kong in modern Chinese history and in a global context (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth).
4. Articulate fair evaluation on issues surrounding the daily life in Hong Kong (e.g. inequalities in economic and political power, housing problem, etc.) after understanding their origins, and able to reflect on how to promote social reform and justice based on the experience of the past (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities and SDG#16 Peace, Justice and Social Institution).

courses.title: Magic, Myth and the Supernatural
courses.description:
(UGEC2960 is double-coded with ANTH2340.)

This course will examine phenomena often viewed as irrational and superstitious to see how they can be understood in cultural terms. All societies have some beliefs in another world, yet beliefs vary widely between societies. The course will examine traditional anthropological topics such as magic, traditional healing, divination, fengshui, witchcraft, and ghosts, as well as more recent issues such as ESP, psychokinesis, qigong, vampires, zombies, monsters, UFOs and alien abduction. The role of myth in modern society and the cultural creation of reality will be highlighted. The power of a cultural approach in explaining the supernatural and the limits of what science can explain will also be discussed.

courses.required_readings:
* *1)****Magic, uncertainty, and rumor**

Gmelch, George "Baseball Magic." In Lehmann and Myers 5'h edition (a revised version) (Also in Spradley & McCurdy 2003, pp. 348-357). [A famous article that discusses magic in sports and introduces the anthropological analysis of magic across cultures.]

* *2)****Urban Legends**

Brunvand, Jan Harold 1981 Chapters 1 & 3 in *The Vanishing Hitchhiker: American Urban Legends and Their Meanings,* pp. 1-16,47-69. [An introduction to urban legends and some famous examples from the USA.]

* *3)****Ghosts and Spirits**

Evans, Grant "Ghosts and the New Governor: The Anthropology of a Hong Kong Rumor." In Grant Evans and Maria Tam Siu-mi, eds. *Hong Kong**: The Anthropology of a Chinese Metropolis,* pp. 267-296. [This is an analysis of the case of the ghost(s) in the 1992 KCR commercial.]

Freed, Stanley A. and Ruth S. Freed "Taraka's Ghost" in Lehmann and Myers (31d ed.) pp. 287-291. (Also in Spradley & McCurdy 2003 *Conformity and Conflict,* pp. 341-347). [This is a famous Indian example of possession by a ghost.]

* *4)****Witchcraft and Evil Eye**

Vurke, Charlanne. "Witchcraft Tswana Style." In James Spradley and David McCurdy *Conformity and Conflict* 11th Edition, pp. 358-370. [An example of contemporary witchcraft in Africa].

Luhrmann, Tanya. "The Goat and the Gazelle: Witchcraft." In William A. Haviland and Robert J. Gordon, eds. *Talking About People: Readings in Contemporary Cultural Anthropology,* pp.232-239. [An example of modern witchcraft in England]

* *5)****Divination**

Hyman, Ray "Cold Reading: How to Convince Strangers That You Know All About Them." In Kendrick Frazier, ed. *Paranormal Borderlands* *of* *Science,* pp. 79-96. [A key article that explains how fortune-telling works]

Rapport, Nigel. 1988. "A Policeman's Construction of 'The Truth': Sergeant Hibbs and the Lie-Detector Machine." *Anthropology Today* 4(1):7-11 (available from the ULI online through JSTOR) [This article shows how the "lie detector" machine is a form of divination. Keep in mind as you read this article that the lie detector is not reliable (though it claims to be scientific), and that the result of the test itself *i*s *not* admissible in court, though if the suspect confesses to the operator, that confession is admissible.]

* *6)****Shamanism**

Howells, William "The Shaman: A Siberian Spiritualist." In Lehmann and Myers (all editions) [This article describes the classic example of shamanism.]

Harner, Michael. 2003 (orig. 1980). "Discovering the Way." In Harvey, Graham, ed. 2003. *Shamanism: A Reader.* New York: Routledge, pp. 41-56. [Harner describes how he was initiated into the practice of shamanism. A good example of the complex combination of pharmacology, cosmology, psychology and sociology of shamanism.]

* *7)****Traditional healing**

Dubisch, Jill "You are What You Eat: Religious Aspects of the Health Food Movement." In Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed. pp. 55-63; 5th edition pp. 73-81). [This article shows how whether something is viewed as "health food" in the US is as much determined by our symbolic system for classifying foods as by biomedical facts.]

Dodes, John E. 1997 "The Mysterious Placebo." *Skeptical Inquirer* 21(1):44-5. [This brief article explains the placebo effect, or how just thinking you are taking a medicine can make you better.]

* *8)****Vampires and Monsters**

Barber, Paul "The Real Vampire" in Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed. pp. 307-3 12) (5th ed. 318-323). [The author discovers that the original stories of vampires in Eastern Europe are based on how the body decomposes. Do not read right after eating!]

Evans, Grant 1993 "Bringing the mermaid myth back to port." (SCMP handout) [A short newspaper article about a rumor about a mermaid in 1993 Hong Kong. Why does the author have to write back to the SCMP after they cut the last paragraph of his article?]

Jones, David E. 2000 Chapter 7 "Fate of the Dragons" in *An Instinct for Dragons* pp. 113-1 19. [The author asks why all cultures have dragons, and why we fear dragons. Do you agree with the author?]

* *9)****UFOs and Alien Abduction**

Huston, Peter 1998 "Night terrors, sleep paralysis, and devil-stricken telephone cords from hell." In Kendrick Frazier, ed. *Encounters with the Paranormal* pp. 294-299. [A short article on vivid images we have as we fall asleep and as we wake up.]

Korff, Kal K. 1997 "What Really Happened at Roswell" *Skeptical Inquirer* 21(4):24-32.

Glidenberg, Bernard D., and David E. Thomas 1998 "Case Closed: Reflections on the 1997 Air Force Roswell Report." *Skeptical Inquirer* 22(3):31-36. [These two articles present the skeptical and official versions of the Roswell case.]

* *10)****Myths**

Bierlein, J. F. 1999 "Myths of Nature and Human Nature" in *Living Myths: How Myth Gives Meaning to Human Experience.* New York: Ballantine.. Pp. 91-98. [This chapter looks at a Greek myth, and teases out some of its meanings]

Campbell, Joseph, 1988 first half of Chapter 5 "The Hero's Adventure" in *The Power of Myth* (with Bill Moyers) pp. 123-140 in large-format version (pp. 151-172 in small font 1991 edition of the book with few illustrations). [This chapter, from a popular book and video (also available at the UC video library) discusses the hero in myth.]

* *11)****Conclusion: "Superstition," Relativism, and Science**

Sagan, Carl "The Burden of Skepticism" in Lehmann and Myers (31d ed. pp. 371-376) *(5th* ed. pp. 384-389). [The late Carl Saga, an astrophysicist, discusses why we must be skeptical, but not be cynical or closed-minded.]

Lewis, I. M. "The Anthropologist's Encounter with the Supernatural." In Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed.) pp. 18-23. [The author, an anthropologist, argues that we can never conclusively exclude the possibility of supernatural beings.]

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Gender in Asia
courses.description:
(UGEC2970 is double-coded with ANTH2330.)

This course focuses on gender in the Asian region. A comparative approach will be taken to reflect diversity and resemblance, continuity and discontinuity, and historical and contemporary influences on gender within countries in the Asian region. Societies studied may vary from year to year, and may include Hong Kong, mainland China, India, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Chinese across societies. Gender issues and conditions will be examined within different contexts, covering such areas as language, class, work, family and kinship, health, sexuality, education, religion, development and politics.

courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students learn to appreciate that in Asia, a vast and culturally diverse region, in an era of globalization and spread of consumerism and tourism, the concepts, roles and relations of gender in Asia are changing rapidly. Students will examine how gender as one of the guiding principles of social life takes various forms in different Asian cultures.

2. Students will learn a cross-cultural perspective to understanding the similarities and differences, as well as the change and continuity in the region.

3. A focus on how gender interacts with the family and marriage will challenge students to rethink taken-for-granted concepts and social behavior, and in the process develop critical thinking on such contested phenomena as public-private divide, the body and the social, religion, ethnicity, and class.

courses.title: Globalization and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2990 is double-coded with ANTH2520.)

Globalization is economically transforming the world, as national borders become increasingly irrelevant before the global flow of money and goods. But globalization also has a great impact on cultures across the globe, as products from Coca-Cola to iPods, and ideas from human rights to ideals of beauty to ideologies of terrorism, intrude everywhere. This course examines how globalization is fundamentally transforming the meanings of culture. The course objectives are to enable students:
(1) to have greater insight into the processes of “the globalization of culture"”, and
(2) to better understand the nature of their own culture and selves within a globalizing world.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Living Feminisms: Creating a Nonviolent and Collaborative Future
courses.description:
(UGEC3204 is double-coded with GDRS3006.)

Living Feminisms is all about how to put feminism into practice. Specifically, it is concerned with living out feminist consciousness in every step of making fundamental and lasting social change. With this in mind, Living Feminisms is not an exposition of feminist theories per se but an exploration of how social change effort would look like when we take up feminist consciousness that transcends separateness and duality. It explores the root causes that lead to the domination system that has plagued humanity for centuries, examines the possibility of having a fundamental and lasting social transformation that supports life of all, and takes a closer look at a few selected alternative practices such as restorative justice and sharing economies that hold out hope in times of crises.

The course also equips students with practical knowledge of being a change agent, introducing some practices with feminist consciousness that transform limiting beliefs about social change, nourish resilience by taking care of social and political trauma, and cultivate need-based facilitation skills and leadership that help navigate conflicts in the process of making internal as well as external transformation. To put it in a nutshell, Living Feminisms is a course that cultivates change agents with feminist consciousness.

Living Feminisms deeply resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 as a blueprint for building a sustainable future by 2030. The course directly touches on alternative practices working towards the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals).

courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will acquire both knowledge and skills of social change that are in line with feminist consciousness. Specifically, they will be able to explain the roots of the domination system and a series of factors contributing to its perpetuation, and able to make change by transforming internal and external resistance. Students will be empowered to take lead in change effort through collaboration with others and mastery of conflict transformation skills. Students will learn to appreciate making a sustainable future requires transformation in areas broader than the conventionally defined economic realm.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Class 1: How We Got Where We Are and Where Are We Heading?**

·Riane Eisler and Douglas P. Fry’s biocultural approach that explains the perpetuation of domination systems through the interaction between genes, brain development and culture, and points to ways where hope lies

* *Class 2: How Change Happens? A Lesson from Feminists**

·Investigating over 100 organizations in 15-year longitudinal research, Aruna Rao et al. develop a model of change that sheds lights on the mechanism of social transformation

·Cristina Bicchieri’s work delves into the formation and change of norms

* *Class 3: What Makes Things Stuck? Inaction Explained**

·How can we explain inaction of people witnessing immense suffering of others? Is the notion of false consciousness adequate? Joanna Macy, a Buddhist scholar and a veteran environmentalist, offers us some glimpse

* *Class 4: *Practice*: Retelling a New Story and Reconnecting to Life that We All Share**

·Understanding the impact of separateness at cognitive level is important but far from complete, Sharif Abdullah and Gretchen Ki Steidle offer us some practical advice on healing the deep-seated separateness by retelling a new story about human beings that fosters interdependence

* *Class 5: Taking Action: Violent or Nonviolent or Both?**

·Taking action to initiate change at various levels of a society is commonplace for activists. What is important is the kinds of action we undertake What is nonviolence? How does it work? What are its limits?

* *Class 6: Social Trauma and Social Transformation**

·Trauma is an overwhelming experience that outweighs the containing capacity of our nervous system How does trauma relate to and shape our political behaviors? Rather individualizing trauma as a single person experiences, how can we theorize collective trauma?

* *Class 7: *Practice*: Self-Care & Inner Resources**

·Change agents are prone to feel despair, powerlessness and hopelessness because they are more acutely aware of the enormity of suffering How to nourish our heart to make it open to pain and suffering while keeping the passion alive?

* *Class 8: Reconciliation and Justice: Exploring Transitional Justice**

·Common collective responses to atrocities are either forgetting or vengeance. Is transitional justice a viable third way? How does it work? What are the experiences of the 40 Truth and Reconciliation Commissions that have ever set up in human history can tell us?

* *Class 9: Sexual Violence: Exploring Restorative Justice**

·Our current justice system is a kind of retribution that punishes those who violate the law. How does it look like if we shift from retribution to restoration that focuses on needs and rebuilding of broken relationships? How controversial is it when applying to sexual violence?

* *Class 10: Collaboration and Feminist Leadership: Coming to Terms with Power**

·Activism often entails working with others. Is power necessarily evil? How does feminist leadership look like? How can we consciously use power in a way that does not subjugate but empower others? How can we replace power-over with power-with, power-to and power-within? Power-cube analysis

* *Class 11: Alternative Organizing - Holacracy, Sociocracy and Deep Democracy**

·There are always implicit agreements as to how to make decisions, define the nature and the scope of a task, evaluate outcome, and handle conflicts if we do not consciously decide how and what to decide

·Quite a many grassroots organizations have been experimenting with new ways of organizing that is more efficient than representative democracy in meeting the needs of all. These alternative forms of governance include Holacracy, Sociocracy and Deep Democracy.

* *Class 12: *Practice*: Workshop on Convergent Facilitation**

·Convergent facilitation, developed by the feminist Miki Kashtan, a form of facilitation that caters for both willingness and efficiency in order to come up an agreement, decision and/or concrete strategies that maximally work for the needs of all within a group. The workshop will cover the whole process from the start to the end convergent facilitation is a proven one as it was applied to a group who disagreed with each other about legalization of abortion

* *Class 13: Beyond Neoliberalism? Sharing Economy**

·Our current economies are profit-driven that more often than not serves a few but exploits most of other people Is it really hopeless to revise capitalism? Is Sharing Economy a viable alternative?

* *Class 14: Conflict Transformation: From the Personal to the International**

Disagreements and conflicts among activists are commonplace. However, acquiring ways of resolving and transforming conflicts within groups is a skill that is urgently needed but seldom given enough attention this last lecture will touch on conflict resolution and mediation.

courses.title: Media Representations of Minorities in Hong Kong
courses.description:
(UGEC3215 is double-coded with GDRS3214.)

How do we understand the notion of “minority”? And how does “minority”, look like, in cinema?

This course examines the rich tradition of critical film theory and provides students with an understanding of its main concerns and debates, concerning “minority” identities and subalternity. Addressing key discussions about media representations of “minority”, the course will look at the politics of representation and its impacts, both on- and off-screen. We will be looking at how media works to construct “the Other” in different contexts, and delve into important work which have inspired minority cinema, subaltern cinema, avant-garde cinema, local cinema, and independent cinema among other counter-movements, as well as recent re-conceptualizations and exploration of representations marginalized identities, positions, and experiences, local and abroad.

This course aims to introduces students to cinematic representations of differences as a productive paradigm of identity politics. While cultural theorist Stuart Hall suggests that identity politics is primarily a representation politics enacted through ever-changing conjunctures of differences, black feminist scholars bell hooks remind us that the margin is an open-ended position to create inside-out and outside-in connections. To examine the representation of minorities is therefore to cultivate an ability to embrace the margins, which allows us to ponder how the construction of “we” can be opened to “they,” the differences. With its divergent forms such as video art, film activism, commercial cinema and film system as well as film festivals, cinema provides a powerful medium for such a task. The question asked throughout the course would be: what are the normative representations of minorities in different forms of cinema? At the production level, to what extent could “minority” artists and theorists rebel against such normative representations—with what alternative visual images and narrative tools? At the level of spectatorship and reception, what kind of reading strategy could generate alternative politics of the minorities? What happened when digital platforms intervene into such endeavors of the minorities?

In the course, we will look at how socially marginalized groups, such as gay and lesbians, transgender persons, ethnic minorities, women in different stages of their lives, people with mental illness, teenagers, the elderly and many others are portrayed, and seek to expand their on-screen existence in Hong Kong media. In the exploration, we will engage with key questions in critical film studies, including spectatorship, authorship, popular culture, character stereotypes in genre films, self-representation, systems of media production, pro-sumer culture, (g)local cinema, alternative cinema, and new media. Students would be introduced to trailblazing works by “minority” filmmakers and media creators worldwide, and important cinematic and media movements that challenge the status-quo. Special focus will be placed onto important works in Hong Kong and Asia for critical examination and comparative studies.

Through critical exercise and reflection on notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

courses.course_syllabus:
1. What is Representation?: A View of the Margins (SDG 5 & 10)

- Setting up the tone of the course by introducing theories and concepts in relation to representations and margins

2. Hong Kong and the Minor (SDG 5 & 10)

- Introducing the idea of minor literature as a state of becoming to contest existing cultural identities and critical theories of Hong Kong

* *Part 1: Forms of Cinema as Media**

3. Engendering Hong Kong Cinema (SDG 5 & 10)

- Brief introduction of the history of Hong Kong cinema with a focus on the gendered and sexual meaning of its overt commercialism

4. A Feminist Reading of Hong Kong’s Independent Cinema (SDG 5 & 10)

- Investigating the ample representations and self-representations of gender and sexual minorities in the independent realm

5. Film Festivals: A Site of Social Actions (SDG 5 & 10)

- Explaining the significance of film festivals in enacting social changes for the minorities

- Introducing the way feminist and queer communities utilise film festivals to achieve their activist goal

* *Part 2: Figures of Minorities**

6. Sexualizing Hong Kong’s In-Betweenness (SDG 5 & 10)

- Examining how representations of sexual minorities construct Hong Kong cinema as a border that both separates Hong Kong from and connect it to East Asia

7. Coming-of-Age in a Postmetropolis (SDG 5 & 10)

- Reckoning with youth as both a status of identity and a representation that ascribes sexual and gender politics in a capitalist city

8. Aging Differently (SDG 5 & 10)

- Studying how the representation of aging serves as an analytical tool by which social inequalities in and the cultural identity of Hong Kong can be interrogated

9. Trans Cinema: Shimmering and Transing (SDG 5 & 10)

- Equipping students with conceptual tools such as aesthetic of shimmering and politics of trans-ing to critically engage with the debate between trans as an identity and non-identity politics

10. Ethnic Minorities: Constructing South Asian Men and Southeast Asian Women (SDG 5 & 10)

- Reflecting on the gendered and sexualized stereotypes of ethnic minorities and the very notion of ethnicity/race in Hong Kong

11. Crippling Cinema: Disability, Gender, and Sexuality (SDG 5 & 10)

- Learning from the representations of the disabled that how able-bodiness underpins our perception of sexualities

12. Are They Also One of Us? New Immigrants, Indigenous People, and Boat People (SDG 10)

- Questioning the boundary of Hong Kong identity by learning the history of the minorities excluded from the mainstream, popular, and official discourse

13. Queer Infrastructure: Mediating Life Within and Beyond Identity Politics (SDG 5 & 10)

- Introducing the queer conception of infrastructure as a living mediation of lifeworlds to prob with the possibilities of envisioning an open-ended Hong Kong’s future

courses.description:
(UGEC3227 is double-coded with GDRS3021.)

This course critically explores the development of LGBTQI+ studies as an interdisciplinary field of inquiry. It traces how LGBTQI+ communities develop against the backdrops of social forces and social oppression. It analyzes the cultural, social and legal environments that LGBTQI+ people live with, in diverse spheres such as families, education, employment, health and the media. The discussions focus on both the structural constraints that LGBTQI+ people face, but also the agency and resilience they display. It explores the development of contemporary LGBTQI+ identities and social movements, as well as the politics involved. The course also asks how gender and sexual diversity is understood in different parts of the world in an era of globalization. Students are also exposed to different practices, policies and laws that are related to LGBTQI+ people’s lives.

The Sustainable Development Goals vow to work towards a society where no one if left behind, particularly those who are most vulnerable and marginalized. In many parts of the world, LGBTQI+ people are historically amongst the most vulnerable and marginalized in society. This course will discuss the unequal treatment they face in cultural, social, political and legal systems and discuss how such inequality may be addressed.

courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, the student will:

- Students are expected to be able to debunk how sexualities and intimacies are shaped by larger social forces and therefore socially constructed.

- Students are expected to be able to analyze the social and historical development of LGBTQI+ identities and communities.

- Students are expected to gain an understanding of LGBTQI+ lives in contemporary societies from empirical examples in diverse spheres of life.

- Students are expected to be able to critically examine how sexualities intersect with other social categories, such as race, ethnicity, class, age and disability;

- Students are expected to critically assess social messages regarding sexualities and intimacies and question the extent to which they themselves agree or disagree with the conventional ‘definitions’ and ‘norms’ in society.

- Students are expected to be able to explore and assess different practice, policy and legal options that are related to LGBTQI+ people’s lives.

courses.title: Understanding Masculinities and Social Change
courses.description:
(UGEC3229 is double-coded with GDRS3007.)

This course examines men’s diverse experiences as boys/men and public discourses and practices about masculinities. It will focus on how the gendered social order influences men’s actions and the way men perceive themselves, other men, women, and social situations. It will pay special attention to the exploration of the relationships between multiple dimensions of social relations and inequalities including gender, race/ethnicity, class, and sexual orientation. It will address issues including but not limited to: male socialization, boyhood, male body images, male friendship, male sexuality and fertility, men’s experiences as fathers, male aggression and violence, men’s commitments to work, men’s social participation, and media representations of boys and men in contemporary culture. It will also explore other forms and interpretations of masculinities, such as female masculinities and queer masculinities, and to investigate to what extent they post challenges to hegemonic masculinity. Students will be introduced to the latest developments and their global networks, and to evaluate the prospects for social change in how men may think, feel, and act otherwise.

The course resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) through critical engagement with different discourses and phenomenon related to masculinities.

courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1**

* *Introduction - Thinking about masculinities**

Key ideas: Introducing critical Masculinities Studies as a field of study, and introduce the history of the development of the discipline

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

* *Week 2**

* *Theorizing masculinities (1): Classic theories**

Key ideas: Introduce classic theories of Masculinities Studies, and familiarise students with important arguments and debates

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 3**

* *Theorizing masculinities (2): New developments**

Key ideas: Based on classic theories, trace debates and new developments in the field

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 4**

* *Education, “salary man” and the delusion of the “masculine promise”: Understanding masculinity in East Asia amidst social-economic change**

Key ideas: Starting with education of boys, talk about the systematic creation of certain idealised mode of “masculinity”, often closely related to life planning along occupational line. Using the case of “salary man” of post-war Japan and Korea, explore the “masculine promise” in East Asia is challenged amidst social-economic change

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

* *Week 5**

* *Masculinity, organization, the masculinization of social change**

Key ideas: Explore the notions of institutionalised masculinity and political masculinity, and how it shapes imaginations of social institutions and social change

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

* *Week 6**

* *Construction of a collective identity: Masculine imaginations of swordsmen and gangsters in Hong Kong cinema**

Key ideas: Using the case of the swordsmen and gangster character in Hong Kong cinema, explore the construction of collective identity along a matric of masculine imaginations of the Hong Kong subject

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

* *Week 7**

* *What makes a man: Penis, dildos, and the challenges of the disembodied Phallus**

Key ideas: Explores the centrality of libido, virility, and sexual performance in the construction and validation of masculinity, and its problems and challenges

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 8**

* *Men on both sides of the sex industry**

Key ideas: Explore how the roles men play in the sex industry, both as sex workers, and consumers of commercialised sex, and its implications on different practices of masculinity

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 9**

* *Mental wellness, self-harm, emotional literacy, and the unique challenges of emotional support for men**

Key ideas: Explore the topic of mental well-being, and its complex relationship with masculinity – how certain beliefs about masculinity could potentially reduce mental well-being, and how culture is increasingly empowering men to have increased emotional literacy and means of expression

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 10**

* *“Boys’ Love” and the reimagining male emotional and sexual potentiality**

Key ideas: Explore how boys’ love culture is opening up cultural space for discussions, explorations, and reimaginations of male emotional and sexual potentiality

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities)

* *Week 11**

* *Masculine ideal and the policing of queer Asian possibilities**

Key ideas: Explore how the centrifugal force of certain dominant notion of masculinity is actively shaping the possibilities of different racial and sexual bodies

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

* *Week 12**

* *Not your cis-hetero-men: Masculinities according to trans man, butches, and drag kings**

Key ideas: Explore how different actors in society are complicating and challenging normative definitions and practices of masculinity, opening up space for discussions, explorations, and reimaginations of multiple masculinities

SDG: 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions)

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Animals, Culture and Modern Society
courses.description:
(UGEC3481 is double-coded with CURE3003.)

How do we understand and connect to animal kingdom?
How do human-animal connections shape modern culture and society?
How do cultural studies and humanities expand our scope on animal and nature?

Culture is ordinary, in Raymond William’s saying, but the ordinariness is merely treated as a reflection of human everyday life. Although cultural studies has sustained concern on everyday life with mass production, consumerism, sexism, racism and postmodernism, the discipline always lags behind the concern of nature and animal species. As the issues of animal abuse, environmental protection, factory farming, animal protection policy and law-making, as well as media various portrayals being the hot topics of our (post)modern world, the study of animal with the perspective of cultural studies and other humanity disciplines can explore the possibilities of better human-animal relationship. This course is designed with an empathic concern of other-than-human animals. By exploring different issues of human and animals’ life, this course looks for a harmonious balance of nature and modern culture.

This course focuses on three areas, through which we can explore the different aspects of animal and cultural studies. These areas are:
A. Entering Jurassic Park – Remaking Animals in Leisure (Lecture A1-A4)
B. Attacking Godzilla – Representing Animals in Media (Lecture B1-B4)
C. Finding Nemo – Revitalizing Animals in the City (Lecture C1-C4)

Each area covers a set of animal issue discussion. Area A, apart from theorizing animal with cultural studies, tackles the basic animal issues: pet-nurturing, zoo-building, forest-sustaining and tourism. This is to provide a foundation for understanding animals with a critical reflection of everyday life.

Area B, set with the concern of media, discusses issues of animal representation in cartoon, cinema, literature and journalism. This is to read how animals would be represented and how this affects human understanding and related policy-making. A screening will be run after Lecture Area B. This is to provide an alternative understanding of animal representation in popular media.

Area C further deals with the matters of animal-city relationship in seeing how dogs and cats, cattle and swine, and fishes and dolphins are (mal)treated in the street, the farm and the sea respectively. This is to end the course with a leading thought of perfect balance of nature and modernity; and more queries of human-animal relationship will be raised for contemplation.

courses.title: Film, Television and Hong Kong Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC3635 is double-coded with COMM3191.)

Since the 1970s, a very distinctive Hong Kong culture has emerged. The course will focus on the role of film and television in the historical formation of this vibrant Hong Kong culture. It will also explore themes such as re-nationalization, nostalgia and representations of mainlanders after the sovereignty transfer in 1997.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC3635 is double-coded with COMM3191. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM3191. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be able to describe key characteristics of Hong Kong films and television in different historical periods.
2. Students will be able to discuss the influences and limitations of mass media in fostering collective identity.
3. Students will be able to differentiate between key concepts such as local and national identities, media representations and social practices, etc.
4. Students will be able to discuss competing viewpoints about the complicated relations between collective memories, cultural identity, and media representations.
5. Students will be able to produce a term paper that offers a critique to one of the ten issues covered in the course.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course will cover ten recurring issues on mediated Hong Kong culture. These issues are intentionally framed as debatable questions. These questions are all leading to the re-thinking of significant and recurring issues of public concerns. Key concepts will be introduced so that students can apply them in formulating their own analyses. The class will also study the competing viewpoints, and their justifications, held by different stakeholders. The sequence of these issues implies a progression of knowledge regarding the ten questions to be asked and answered in the course.

The following is an outline of the course:

(1) Introduction: The formation of Hong Kong Culture, a historical overview
The lecture will trace the formation and changes of Hong Kong culture from the 1950s to the 2010s, relating social changes to the cultural changes of audio-visual texts produced in different periods of time. Key concepts will be introduced to help students make sense of cultural patterns as articulated in movies and television programs.
Key concepts: textuality, contextuality, media representations

(2) The Birth of Hong Kong Man
The lecture will focus on the cultural differentiations of mainlanders and Hongkongers in the 1970s. Students will think about the question of why Hong Kong people, mostly ethnic Chinese, saw themselves as a rather different social group of their own. A few classic texts will be used to illustrate the logic of "othering" and stigmatizing mainlanders.
Key concepts: "other", cultural imaginations, stigma

(3) New Wave Film and Colonial Politics
The lecture will introduce some basic concepts of colonialism. Some mainstream texts will be contrasted with some new wave movies of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Some patterns of colonial articulations and de-articulations will be illustrated by these mainstream and new wave productions.
Key concepts: colonialism, marginality

(4) Political Metaphors in TV and Film
The lecture will explain the reasons why there were quite of lot of political metaphors in television and films produced in the 1990s. The relations between political censorship, social anxiety and polysemic articulations will be elaborated with significant cases.
Key concepts: polysemy, metaphor, censorship

(5) Nonsense and Nostalgia, Remembering and Forgetting
The lecture will explain the nature of mediated collective memories and the social functions they perform. The rise of nostalgic texts in the 1990s will be contrasted with the discourses of collective memories in the 2000s.
Key concepts: nostalgia, collective memories

(6) Urban Space & Postmodern City
The lecture will trace the changes in urban representations in films and television from the 1980s up to recent years when discourses concerning urban developments and cultural preservations are competing for public attention.
Key concepts: urban imaginations, postmodernity, space and place

(7) Media Events: 1997 and 1st July
The lecture will introduce the theory of "media events" and apply it to major turning points of Hong Kong society such as July 1st in 1997 and 2003, SARS, the Sichuan earthquake, etc. The changes of Hong Kong culture will be examined by looking into the configurations of major media events in recent years.
Key concepts: media events, social movements

(8) The Rise & Fall of the HK Middle Class
The lecture will trace the "middle class debate" in the 1980s. Students will be asked to think about their own class positions and how they acquired a class-relevant lifestyle. The changes in media representations of the middle class will be analyzed to see how these representations have become more sophisticated since the 1990s.
Key concepts: middle class, cultural capitals, taste

(9) Post 97 Hong Kong Culture
The lecture will summarize some major changes in Hong Kong cultures after 1997 and contrast these new patterns with the cultural scene before 1997, focusing on the negotiations of local and national identifications.
Key concepts: re-sinicization, nationalism

(10) Transborder and Transnational Desire
The lecture will tell the story of the Hong Kong/Mainland border and the cultural politics it brings to the people on both sides of the border. As cultural differentials have been lowered in recent years, the general categorizations of them and us are replaced by much more complicated transborder collaborations infused with excitements and apprehensions.
Key concepts: transborder cultural politcs, border, cultural boundaries

(11) Undercover Films: the double identity of Hong Kong
Using films featuring under-covered agents, the lecture will talk about the multiple identity of Hong Kong, relating this issue to Hong Kong colonial history and the political structure of one country and two systems.
Key concepts: collaborative colonialism, instrumental rationality

(12) Orientalism: Hong Kong, Hollywood and Beyond
The lecture will use Hong Kong movie star Chow Yuen-fat as a case to examine the rise and changes of Hong Kong culture. The "star-text" of Chow will be used to illustrate the effects of Orientalism, comparing Chow's local films and those produced in Hollywood.
Key concepts: orientalism, star text

(13) The decline of local films and the rise of co-productions
The lecture will document the trends of co-productions and examine the effects on the weakening of local representations and the amplifications of national imaginations.
Key concepts: de-scaling, re-scaling, local scale, national scale

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Introduction to Global Sociology
courses.description:
(UGEC3893 is double-coded with SOCI3241.)
This course introduces undergraduate students to the knowledge world of global and transnational sociology, and the sociology of law, globalization and global governance, in which it will offer a guided entry into the complex ideas and writings of the sociological, political and legal scholars. The concepts they developed to analyze law, society and global governance are fundamental to address global and international concerns, including ESG (environmental, social & governance) investment, SDG (sustainable development goals), global climate change (Paris Agreement), global health (WHO), international economic, trade and monetary institutions (e.g., World Bank, WTO, IMF), global gender, children, labor and human rights systems (UNICEF, ILO, OHCHR), international law (ICJ) and international peace and security (UN Security Council). Upon completing this course, student will have critical understanding of the process in which UN intergovernmental bodies, states and non-governmental stakeholders coordinate at the inter-organizational and inter-institutional levels to implement the UN 2030 Agenda, and respond to the challenges within.

courses.course_syllabus:
Topic 1: Introduction to Global and Transnational Sociology

Topic 2: Theory and Methods – Fieldwork, Ethnography and Participant Observation

* Question: How does the concept of exchange evolve from Mauss and Malinowski to Lévi-Strauss, Bourdieu, Fei Xiaotong and Dezalay? /中外学者如何抽象学术问题？

Topic 3: Theory and Methods – Historical/Economic/Institutional Sociology and Sociolegal Studies

* Question: How do academic scholars conduct global, transnational or comparative studies? /中外学者如何进行全球/跨国比较研究？

Topic 4: Global Law-Making and International Organizations (IOs) (SDG16, 17)

* Question: Why IOs are so relevant in global, transnational or comparative studies?

SDGs: the topic will enhance students’ knowledge in order to make sense of IOs and their custodianship of various sustainable development goals

Topic 5: Global Economy – Global Empire/World Bank

* Question: Who controls the World Bank and the IMF? What is the difference between the British and American Empires? And, why do the World Bank and IMF matter to an international financial hub like London, New York or Hong Kong?

Topic 6: International Money and Banking – IMF

* Question: who manages the global financial system? What is a financial crisis? And, how did it impact on international financial hubs like London, New York or Hong Kong?

Topic 7: Global Health and Education – WHO, MSF, and UNESCO (SDG3, 4)

* Question: what are the social factors of global health/education inequality?
* SDGs: the topic will examine the role of IOs that promote inclusive and equitable quality education and health and well-being.

Topic 8: International Trade and Investment – WTO and ICSID

* Question: What is the meaning of a free port? Why is it so important for Hong Kong to keep a free port trade policy? How did the US-China trade wars occur? What is the impact of the US-China trade wars on Hong Kong?

Topic 9: International Security and Peace – UNSC, IAEA, OPCW, and others (SDG16, 17)

* Question: what is the impact of UNSC on Hong Kong’s international banking system?
* SDGs: the topic will give the students a rare perspective towards how Hong Kong’s role as a financial centre can help achieve global security targets.

Topic 10: International Law and Justice – ICJ, ICC, ICTY, IOMed (SDG16, 17)

* Question: Why IOMed/ICC is interested in setting up an office in East Asia?
* SDGs: the topic will discuss how international partnership is core to achieving global security targets.

Topic 11: Gender, Children, Labor and Human Rights (SDG5, 8, 16)

* Question: what are the functions of global human rights bodies in the global community?
* SDGs: the topic will explore pathways towards enhancing gender equality, institutionalizing descent work settings and reducing crime and violence.

Topic 12: Global Climate Change and the Paris Agreement (SDG13)

* Question: what are the expected roles of Hong Kong and Mainland China in global action to climate change?
* SDGs: the topic will provide students a up-to-date view of the policy mechanism to achieve climate action targets in the region.

Topic 13: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (SDG17)

* Question: what are the expected roles of Hong Kong and Mainland China in ESG/SDGs?
* SDGs: as a summary, the topic will examine the institutionalization of SDGs in the case of a Chinese society

courses.description:
(UGEC3928 is double-coded with LING3208.)
This survey course introduces non-clinical students to fundamental concepts of language disorders in paediatric and adult populations. Characteristics of primary language impairment, aphasia, dysarthria, and hearing impairments, as well as articulation, fluency, and voice and other related disorders affecting language are among the topics to be discussed. Diagnostic techniques and treatment strategies are also introduced.

Discussions will be made on the impacts of language impairment on one’s cognitive development, academic performance, as well as physical, psychological and social well-being across the lifespan (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being). Students will be able to gain a better understanding of how people suffering from these disorders are deprived from healthy lives (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being), quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth), and social equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities). Students will also come to appreciate the benefits brought by the relevant assessment and treatment in promoting personal wellbeing (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being), ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), providing full and productive employment and decent work for all (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth), as well as reducing inequality in the society (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities).

courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course, students will be able to

* Describe the fundamentals of language and communication, and basic characteristics of language disorders
* Explain the etiology of different language disorders
* Analyze patient signs and symptoms and attribute them to specific language disorder types, and reflect on how these disorders may create barriers to quality education for children (SDG#4 Quality Education) and decent work for adults (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth)
* Identify and analyze the problems brought by language disorders with respect to good health and wellbeing (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being), quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), decent work (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth), and inequality reduction (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)
* Investigate how the diagnostic techniques and treatment strategies can serve to solve the problems brought by language disorders, including those from disadvantaged backgrounds (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)
* Evaluate the difficulties and challenging in implementing assessment and treatment for language disorders for all peoples (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)
* Reflect on the role they can play in promoting wellbeing for all members of the society regardless of their visible and invisible limitations to participate in society (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Foundations of language and communication**

* Systems of communication, classification of disorders

* *Biological foundations of language**

* Anatomy & physiology of the vocal mechanism and the brain

* *Psychometrics, normalcy & variation in language development and functions (SDG#3, #4, #8, #10)**

* Stages of speech, language, and literacy development

* *Speech disorders (SDG#3, #4, #8, #10)**

* Articulation & phonological disorders in children, fluency disorders, voice disorders, and dysarthria
* Characteristics, assessment, and treatment
* Associations between language problems and cognitive development/well-being (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
* Problems brought by speech disorders on quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth) and economic equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)

* *Language disorders in children (SDG#3, #4, #8, #10)**

* Primary language impairment, literacy problem, and genetic syndromes
* Characteristics, assessment, and treatment
* Associations between language problems and cognitive development (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
* Problems brought by language disorders on quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth) and economic equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)

* *Neurogenic disorders in adults (SDG#3, #8, #10)**

* Aphasia and cognitive-based communication disorders
* Characteristics, assessment, and treatment
* Associations between language problems and cognitive well-being (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
* Problems brought by neurogenic disorders on employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth) and economic equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)

* *Hearing impairment and language (SDG#3, #4, #8, #10)**

* Deafness, cochlear implant, and aging
* Characteristics, assessment, and treatment
* Associations between language problems and cognitive well-being (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
* Problems brought by hearing impairment on employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth) and economic equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)

* *Disorders in multi-lingual speakers (SDG#3, #4, #8, #10)**

* Characteristics, assessment, and treatment
* Associations between language problems and cognitive well-being (SDG#3 Good Health and Well-Being)
* Problems brought by language disorders on quality education (SDG#4 Quality Education), employment opportunities (SDG#8 Decent Work and Economic Growth) and economic equality (SDG#10 Reduced Inequalities)
